[{:db/id 17592186119942 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1889a049-4ef8-5003-97ad-4734948ea194" "question-000ec056-1962-5b34-98db-f72ea83a397c" "question-c1e71946-3589-5a14-87c2-2599e8aef444"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-1889a049-4ef8-5003-97ad-4734948ea194" :question/id #uuid "1889a049-4ef8-5003-97ad-4734948ea194" :question/math-academy-id "q-14553" :question/problem "Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-8}{{x}^{2}+x-20}.$" :question/worked-solution "If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-8}{{x}^{2}+x-20} & =\frac{{4}^{2}-2(4)-8}{{4}^{2}+4-20}=\frac{0}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-8}{{x}^{2}+x-20} & =\frac{(x+2)(x-4)}{(x+5)(x-4)} \\  & =\frac{x+2}{x+5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-8}{{x}^{2}+x-20} & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{x+2}{x+5} \\  & =\frac{4+2}{4+5} \\  & =\frac{6}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9da39b9f-c278-5623-b8c6-2f09872d7126"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id -4}\frac{{t}^{2}-16}{{t}^{2}+4t}.$" :question/worked-solution "If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{{t}^{2}-16}{{t}^{2}+4t} & =\frac{(-4)^{2}-16}{(-4)^{2}+4(-4)}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{t}^{2}-16}{{t}^{2}+4t} & =\frac{(t+4)(t-4)}{t(t+4)} \\  & =\frac{t-4}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to -4}\frac{{t}^{2}-16}{{t}^{2}+4t} & ={lim}_{t\to -4}\frac{t-4}{t} \\  & =\frac{-4-4}{(-4)} \\  & =\frac{(-8)}{(-4)} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d2177b68-63d5-53b3-a804-f2a9f09d50af"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 5}\frac{{x}^{2}-5x}{{x}^{2}-8x+15}.$" :question/worked-solution "If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{{x}^{2}-5x}{{x}^{2}-8x+15} & =\frac{{5}^{2}-5(5)}{{5}^{2}-8(5)+15}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-5x}{{x}^{2}-8x+15} & =\frac{x(x-5)}{(x-5)(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{x}{x-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{{x}^{2}-5x}{{x}^{2}-8x+15} & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{x}{x-3} \\  & =\frac{5}{5-3} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}

:question/id #uuid "7aab1343-37d9-52dc-ba1f-d0f44020bf1c" :question/math-academy-id "q-140416" :question/problem "Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{3}-27}{2x-6}.$" :question/worked-solution "If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{3}-27}{2x-6} & =\frac{{3}^{3}-27}{2(3)-6}=\frac{27-27}{6-6}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. 

Notice that the numerator is a difference of cubes. Therefore, factoring our expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{3}-27}{2x-6} & =\frac{{x}^{3}-{3}^{3}}{2(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{(x-3)({x}^{2}+3x+{3}^{2})}{2(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+3x+9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{3}-27}{2x-6} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}+3x+9}{2} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{2}+3(3)+9}{2} \\  & =\frac{9+9+9}{2} \\  & =\frac{27}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-81caaad2-536e-533e-be45-81a17e89437b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-a0beb016-ee67-53e9-a1ae-c396296738c8"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096583 :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}-8{x}^{2}+8x & =0 \\ 2x({x}^{2}-4x+4) & =0 \\ 2x(x-2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=0$ and $x=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x(2{x}^{3}-8{x}^{2}+8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{4}-8{x}^{3}+8{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{4}-4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-{x}^{4}+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =4\pi [(\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}-{2}^{4}+\frac{4\cdot {2}^{3}}{3})-0] \\  & =4\pi [(\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}-\frac{{2}^{5}}{2}+\frac{{2}^{5}}{3})-0] \\  & =4\pi \cdot {2}^{5}(\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =4\pi \cdot 32(\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{64\pi }{15}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096829 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1d5c9e76-b23d-5f4b-b9c9-3236b501399a" "question-dc6488b4-82a0-5ac0-9b15-2d4fb9f9b1f5" "question-4022977e-c101-551c-847a-d892e1fa6f2e" "question-4ae3570d-9f53-5028-8c3b-4778adbb6463"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096584 :question/problem "Consider the finite region bounded between the curves $y=3x-x^2$ and $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2.$ Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(x)=3x-x^2$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}x^2.$ 

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ 3x-{x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} \\ 3x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 2x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(2-x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=0$ and $x=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower and upper functions.

![](images/5a/5a9fd40682646575ada14297ef7e1de766852f99dbdab986d5baa1fb5c2feb94.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=g(x)=\dfrac12 x^2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=f(x)=3x-x^2.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be calculated as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x([\text{upper}]-[\text{lower}])\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x([3x-{x}^{2}]-[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}])\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x(3x-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x(x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x(\frac{2x}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =3\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x(2x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =3\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(2{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & =3\pi {(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =3\pi [(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{16}{4})-0] \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-0dfc8af8-b45c-5404-a021-aa0515c46816" :question/id #uuid "0dfc8af8-b45c-5404-a021-aa0515c46816" :question/math-academy-id "q-352254" :question/problem "Consider the finite region bounded by the curve $y=-4+5x-{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis. Calculate the volume $V$ of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4+5x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=1$ and $x=4.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=1$ to $x=4.$  

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

The solutions are $x=0,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2$ because we are only concerned about $x\ge 0.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower and upper functions.

![](images/cc/ccbaa663f6f108322f7bafd4a192a5b9acdf913b61b8319048e92b7885458a91.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=g(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{4},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=f(x)=x.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x([\text{upper}]-[\text{lower}])\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x([x]-[\frac{{x}^{3}}{4}])\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x(x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{4})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-59f2f9fb-5153-5952-bf13-386d35bef9ea"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "4ae3570d-9f53-5028-8c3b-4778adbb6463" :question/math-academy-id "q-352642" :question/problem "Consider the finite region bounded between the curves $y=\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x$ and $y=-{x}^{3}+\frac{7}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x.$ Calculate the volume $V$ of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(x)=\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x$ and $g(x)=-{x}^{3}+\frac{7}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ \frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x & =-{x}^{3}+\frac{7}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x \\ 3{x}^{2}+5x & =-2{x}^{3}+7{x}^{2}+5x \\ 2{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=0$ and $x=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$

Now, let's draw our usual vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower and upper functions.

![](images/d1/d19b70836b7b377c498fa505868563115706b588b0a2216d09c6ec738f746bbd.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=f(x)=\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=g(x)=-{x}^{3}+\frac{7}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x([\text{upper}]-[\text{lower}])\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x([-{x}^{3}+\frac{7}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x]-[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x])\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x(-{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(-{x}^{4}+2{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {(-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{2})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\pi [(-\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{2}^{4}}{2})-0] \\  & =2\pi (-\frac{32}{5}+8) \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{8}{5} \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2c67a319-c85c-5918-8f19-cbfe5ceda96a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2c67a319-c85c-5918-8f19-cbfe5ceda96a" :answer-field/id #uuid "2c67a319-c85c-5918-8f19-cbfe5ceda96a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-820ac9df-49d1-590e-bc4c-409a7349c4d7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-820ac9df-49d1-590e-bc4c-409a7349c4d7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-820ac9df-49d1-590e-bc4c-409a7349c4d7" :answer/id #uuid "820ac9df-49d1-590e-bc4c-409a7349c4d7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{16\pi}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097882 :tutorial/content "Consider the plane region enclosed by the curve $y=f(x),$ the $x$-axis, and the vertical lines $x=a$ and $x=b,$ as shown below. If we rotate this region $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis, we get a solid of revolution.

![](images/e9/e9902ba13717e576f07a15396e6a78fd823a3ad92762688d7802cc7ac95849c0.png)

We can compute the volume of the solid using the shell method. We divide the interval from $x=a$ to $x=b$ on the $x$-axis to get vertical slices. Consider one such slice of width $\Delta{x},$ as shown in the picture below (on the left). When this rectangle is rotated about the $y$-axis, it forms a solid shell (i.e., the skin of a cylinder).

![](images/c7/c7be68342d347b8ef48e3cf2b8e20b88bedca594fc3d4846f03b5391ae8dbfc2.png)

Since we assume that $\Delta{x}$ is very small, the outer radius of the shell approximately equals the inner radius $x.$ The thickness of the shell is $\Delta{x}$ and its height is $y=f(x)$.

Imagine we cut this shell and unfold it to obtain a rectangular solid, as shown below. Its height is $y=f(x)$, its thickness is $\Delta{x},$ and its length is $2\pi x$ (the circumference of the shell).

![](images/a4/a40f23b110ab24c55665784219b7013e587487f88d8d7857260458b9c7a20d2d.png)

 

The volume of the shell approximately equals the volume of the rectangular solid:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{shell}} & ≈{V}_{\text{rec}} \\  & =2\pi x\cdot y\cdot Δx \\  & =2\pi xf(x)Δx\end{aligned}
$$

The sum of all the shells will approximate the total volume we want. This approximation becomes more accurate as $\Delta{x} \to 0$. Therefore, the volume $V$ of the solid is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}xy\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097883 :tutorial/content "Consider the region enclosed by the curves $y=f(x)$ on the top, $y=g(x)$ on the bottom, and the vertical lines $x=a$ and $x=b,$ as shown below. We assume that $f(x) \geq g(x)$ for all $x \in [a,b].$     

![](images/37/372ece19360ca4f48a5ef48637e49d8f401ee2f1fd562f13c481c767a536bf6c.png)

To find the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis, we use the shell method as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x([\text{upper}]-[\text{lower}])\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x([f(x)]-[g(x)])\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097884 :tutorial/content "One of the advantages of using the shell method versus other methods is that the resulting integral can be much simpler to evaluate. This is often true when we want to rotate a curve of the form $y = f(x)$ about the $y$-axis.

For example, suppose we want to compute the volume generated when the region below is rotated about the $y$-axis:

![](images/ad/ad563abd1e7f4a413337dc9527d2c3703d4851e756f385a75797c6f5962cf51f.png)

According to the shell method, the volume $V$ is given by the following straightforward integral: 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}xf(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x(2x-2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now compare this to the disc method.

To determine the volume using the disc method, we would first have to express our curve as two functions of $y,$ one for the right-hand side and one for the left-hand side, as follows: 

![](images/a8/a841ed797699e8f20b494baa6ff888eb42ccd4715e17733e495405df5ca8c5dc.svg)

![](images/ee/ee7ef70a2a280c42ceea9dc6b8bdb3e3bafbfec0256350cbabde287d33d9884b.png)

The required volume equals the difference between the volumes generated when the right and left curves are rotated about the $y$-axis. Thus, according to the disc method, the required volume is given by

$$
V = \pi \int_{0}^{1/2} \left( \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-2y} \right]^2 - \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-2y} \right]^2 \right) \textrm{d}y.
$$

As we can see, this integral is a lot more complicated than the one we obtained using the shell method!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096873 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073810 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-52deb492-2c28-55be-ad12-3e097a96cc24"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-52deb492-2c28-55be-ad12-3e097a96cc24" :question/id #uuid "52deb492-2c28-55be-ad12-3e097a96cc24" :question/math-academy-id "q-114324" :question/problem "Find the shortest distance between the point $(4,-1)$ and the line $x=-2.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's sketch the given situation.

![](images/ae/ae9c7b44a3e246fb6e0e9f90c1288ef42814c22d705c944e46fe0eb890a5a998.png)

Since the line $x=-2$ is a vertical line, the shortest distance between this line and the point $(4,-1)$ is given by the absolute value of the difference between the $x$-coordinate of the point and $-2.$

Find the point on the line $y=\frac{4}{3}x$ that is closest to the point $(-1,7).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=\frac{4}{3}x$ and passes through the point $(-1,7).$

 The given line has a slope of $\frac{4}{3},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $-\frac{3}{4}.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-7 & =-\frac{3}{4}(x+1) \\ y-7 & =-\frac{3}{4}x-\frac{3}{4} \\ y & =-\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{25}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{4}{3}x \\ y=-\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{25}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3}x & =-\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{25}{4} \\ \frac{4}{3}x+\frac{3}{4}x & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \frac{25}{12}x & =\frac{25}{4} \\ x & =\frac{25}{4}\cdot \frac{12}{25} \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=3$ into either of the two equations gives $y=4.$ So, our solution is $x=3$ and $y=4.$ Therefore, the lines intersect at the point $(3,4).$

Therefore, we conclude that the point on the line $y=\frac{4}{3}x$ that is closest to the point $(-1,7)$ is $(3,4).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields :question/worked-solution "Let's draw a diagram describing our situation. 

![](images/80/80f3e7d79f84a3894e563c78747e22ccf11c889783c39ed6fb688a4242160d60.png)

 

First, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=x+1$ and passes through the point $(3,2).$

 The given line has a slope of $1,$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $-1.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-2 & =-1(x-3) \\ y-2 & =-x+3 \\ y & =-x+5\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=x+1 \\ y=-x+5\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =-x+5 \\ x+x & =-1+5 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=2$ into either of the two equations gives $y=3.$ So, our solution is $x=2$ and $y=3.$ Therefore, the lines intersect at the point $(2,3).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(3,2)$ and $(2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2-3)^{2}+(3-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the shortest distance between the point $(3,2)$ and the line $y=x+1$ is $\sqrt{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields :question/worked-solution "Let's draw a diagram describing our situation. 

![](images/52/52bfc27007c57351cdf90d88d444676266edc5d2704314db0d99fd9dca8e367f.png)

 

First, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=-\frac{2}{3}x+2$ and passes through the point $(8,1).$

 The given line has a slope of $-\frac{2}{3},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $\frac{3}{2}.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =\frac{3}{2}(x-8) \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x-12+1 \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x-11\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=-\frac{2}{3}x+2 \\ y=\frac{3}{2}x-11\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}x+2 & =\frac{3}{2}x-11 \\ -\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{3}{2}x & =-11-2 \\ -\frac{13}{6}x & =-13 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=6$ into either of the two equations gives $y=-2.$ So, our solution is $x=6$ and $y=-2.$ Therefore, the lines intersect at the point $(6,-2).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(8,1)$ and $(6,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(6-8)^{2}+(-2-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+9} \\  & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the shortest distance between the point $(8,1)$ and the line $y=-\frac{2}{3}x+2$ is $\sqrt{13}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1932c306-3c23-58d3-a967-76e055fcd6ec"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1932c306-3c23-58d3-a967-76e055fcd6ec" :answer-field/id #uuid "1932c306-3c23-58d3-a967-76e055fcd6ec" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3be87dbe-29dc-5043-9a79-a86b2fd5a880" :answer-field/choices ["answer-781f5f51-a2bb-5ef5-9600-e203136f5055" "answer-635a77b6-fd8f-5cf2-8d7f-1598dc609b88" "answer-6e1c0892-2c18-5576-a828-53b1cfdefbaf" "answer-4c39f4de-1a6a-52cf-8624-125d851fe285" "answer-3be87dbe-29dc-5043-9a79-a86b2fd5a880"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-781f5f51-a2bb-5ef5-9600-e203136f5055" :answer/id #uuid "781f5f51-a2bb-5ef5-9600-e203136f5055" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-635a77b6-fd8f-5cf2-8d7f-1598dc609b88" :answer/id #uuid "635a77b6-fd8f-5cf2-8d7f-1598dc609b88" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6e1c0892-2c18-5576-a828-53b1cfdefbaf" :answer/id #uuid "6e1c0892-2c18-5576-a828-53b1cfdefbaf" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4c39f4de-1a6a-52cf-8624-125d851fe285" :answer/id #uuid "4c39f4de-1a6a-52cf-8624-125d851fe285" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5\sqrt{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3be87dbe-29dc-5043-9a79-a86b2fd5a880" :answer/id #uuid "3be87dbe-29dc-5043-9a79-a86b2fd5a880" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{13}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186075027 :tutorial/content "Consider the line $l$ with the equation $y=-x + 6$ and the point $Q(2,1)$ that does not lie on $l.$

![](images/83/8353825890413432e74d30512219cb95edc76fe8c24e7a824d6893c745c48bd1.png)

Suppose we wish to find the point $P$ that lies on $l$ that's closest to the point $(2,1).$ 

![](images/f8/f880cfde6bdfe07c6804609f9b052189632afcde4907207de5245298aea9ea6e.png)

Now, here's the key idea: $P$ is the point that lies on $l$ *and* lies on the line *perpendicular* to $l$ that passes through $Q.$

So, to find $P,$ we proceed as follows:

- First, we find the line perpendicular to $l$ that passes through $Q.$

- Then, we find the intersection of the two lines.

The line $y=-x + 6$ has a slope of $-1,$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $1$ (the negative reciprocal). It also must pass through the point $(2,1).$ So, using point-slope form, we find that the equation of the perpendicular line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =1\cdot (x-2) \\ y-1 & =x-2 \\ y & =x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find where the lines $y=-x+6$ and $y=x-1$ intersect, we set the equations equal to each other and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+6 & =x-1 \\ 6+1 & =x+x \\ 7 & =2x \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$ into either of the two equations gives $y=\dfrac{5}{2}.$ So, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left( \dfrac{7}{2}, \dfrac{5}{2} \right).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073946 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186229131 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b6b0c13d-ace9-58a0-a5ae-835939f481e0" "question-ed2f4962-bfe0-5321-8b55-e0e1d5307252"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186229663 :question/problem "$$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t-s} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t-s} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186228180 :answer-field/correct "answer-a71f00de-08de-5313-af96-a181750eb6ae" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a71f00de-08de-5313-af96-a181750eb6ae"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a71f00de-08de-5313-af96-a181750eb6ae" :answer/id #uuid "a71f00de-08de-5313-af96-a181750eb6ae" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e^{2t-s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186228181 :answer-field/correct "answer-ba920ad2-32c3-5075-8ddb-cb1965fbe9d9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ba920ad2-32c3-5075-8ddb-cb1965fbe9d9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ba920ad2-32c3-5075-8ddb-cb1965fbe9d9" :answer/id #uuid "ba920ad2-32c3-5075-8ddb-cb1965fbe9d9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2e^{2t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b6b0c13d-ace9-58a0-a5ae-835939f481e0" :question/id #uuid "b6b0c13d-ace9-58a0-a5ae-835939f481e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-334926" :question/problem "$$

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$

$$

Therefore, we get

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5681283e-4465-523e-8b0e-208f5dbcb496" "answer-field-c5f719c4-a5bf-542d-85f1-a0d87e09bdf0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5681283e-4465-523e-8b0e-208f5dbcb496" :answer-field/id #uuid "5681283e-4465-523e-8b0e-208f5dbcb496" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-37a88885-e7e0-5479-b8d2-d85e774bbf74" :answer-field/choices ["answer-37a88885-e7e0-5479-b8d2-d85e774bbf74"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-37a88885-e7e0-5479-b8d2-d85e774bbf74" :answer/id #uuid "37a88885-e7e0-5479-b8d2-d85e774bbf74" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e^{2s}\cos(2(t-s))" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c5f719c4-a5bf-542d-85f1-a0d87e09bdf0" :answer-field/id #uuid "c5f719c4-a5bf-542d-85f1-a0d87e09bdf0" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-814c0838-d0d0-5c60-bb5d-d662eb334c3a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-814c0838-d0d0-5c60-bb5d-d662eb334c3a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-814c0838-d0d0-5c60-bb5d-d662eb334c3a" :answer/id #uuid "814c0838-d0d0-5c60-bb5d-d662eb334c3a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3\sin(2(t-1))+\cos(2(t-1))" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ed2f4962-bfe0-5321-8b55-e0e1d5307252" :question/id #uuid "ed2f4962-bfe0-5321-8b55-e0e1d5307252" :question/math-academy-id "q-334928" :question/problem "$$

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -{e}^{s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -{e}^{s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3eb19d6e-883e-50f6-b7d5-7815f100a541" "answer-field-4a78e8e2-e93a-5656-bb35-a08702392163"] :db/ensure :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186262737 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/54/5497f23e51d1e745fef1cf39d6c1a8ada22b25e8c9c7b87f5d5338e85a941739.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}x$ and $Q(x,y)=-{y}^{2}x+{y}^{4}.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2yx+{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2yx+4{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-3\le x\le -1,\,-1\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2yx+{y}^{3})+(-2yx+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{-1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}5{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-512baac6-6af2-5983-be4f-040d5e0743f6" :question/id #uuid "512baac6-6af2-5983-be4f-040d5e0743f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-127327" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3},\,\sqrt[3]{x}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/fa/fa98f3db31860a463d0a551d5297895e61a6c041d852c04de04c44a194510961.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}y+x)\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[((1)^{3}y+1)-((-1)^{3}y+(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2y+2)\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{2}+2y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =((2)^{2}+2(2))-0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dcc96fea-c51a-5b5e-9f54-45e9c86734fe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-dcc96fea-c51a-5b5e-9f54-45e9c86734fe" :answer-field/id #uuid "dcc96fea-c51a-5b5e-9f54-45e9c86734fe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-7b1a18cf-57e7-594a-bab2-ece7b5646c56" :answer-field/choices ["answer-44289665-fb34-50eb-942c-684dbafac462" "answer-675393a7-a22d-52c0-8122-89d84461848c" "answer-5d52696f-f66a-5483-9d31-ad3010ca9bf6" "answer-42f7866a-874a-59e8-98df-e82497daf28c" "answer-7b1a18cf-57e7-594a-bab2-ece7b5646c56"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-44289665-fb34-50eb-942c-684dbafac462" :answer/id #uuid "44289665-fb34-50eb-942c-684dbafac462" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-675393a7-a22d-52c0-8122-89d84461848c" :answer/id #uuid "675393a7-a22d-52c0-8122-89d84461848c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5d52696f-f66a-5483-9d31-ad3010ca9bf6" :answer/id #uuid "5d52696f-f66a-5483-9d31-ad3010ca9bf6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-42f7866a-874a-59e8-98df-e82497daf28c" :answer/id #uuid "42f7866a-874a-59e8-98df-e82497daf28c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7b1a18cf-57e7-594a-bab2-ece7b5646c56" :answer/id #uuid "7b1a18cf-57e7-594a-bab2-ece7b5646c56" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186262759 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/34/3497b3bbc834879026235f97468f5feb26e91a2b73a4de3da87597bf422ecd33.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)-y{x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+2xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x-2xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{2}-{x}^{2}y)\,{|}_{0}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[(1-y)-0]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(1-y)\,dy \\  & =[y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-((-1)-\frac{(-1)^{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186262757 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

![](images/ea/ea6c25e40b6683d9ff4a4884dbbda708fd79dbd79d0b50730f9ad6e165d2eb58.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{y}+x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-6{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(1-6{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-2{x}^{3}y)\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(2-2(2)^{3}y)-0]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2-16y)\,dy \\  & =[2y-8{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(2(1)-8(1)^{2})-0 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186262754 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

We have that $P(x,y)=6y{x}^{2}+{e}^{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=3{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186262758 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$

which is equivalent to

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

We have that $P(x,y)=6{x}^{2}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)=-10y-\operatorname{arctan}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=12x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-2y\le x\le 2y,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(12x-10)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2y}^{2y}(12x-10)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[6{x}^{2}-10x]_{-2y}^{2y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(24{y}^{2}-20y)-(24{y}^{2}+20y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-40y)\,dy \\  & =-40{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-40(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186262755 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/c4/c4dd4d03bdfcf6c3d597e2fdef8681e4f3316b3f276cb9967933b61b0dc90976.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x-\sqrt{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=y-\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dx \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2(0-(-1)) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186262760 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/00/006d80a7dbe4d03b78cc5fb1a642405e3fdfdd69ec9d80014ee8e0355ad1ae73.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{y}{2},\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y/2}^{y/2}(y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[x]_{-y/2}^{y/2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[\frac{y}{2}-(-\frac{y}{2})]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}+y)\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{4}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083387 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-761ee71b-75fd-5326-b76e-466bf3a8a311"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186082953 :question/problem "Consider the quadratic equation

$$
8x^2 + 5x - 12 = 0.
$$

**Without** solving the equation, determine the sum of its solutions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
ax^2 + bx + c = 0
$$

has the solutions $x = x_1$ and $x = x_2,$ where $a\neq 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

For the given quadratic equation, we have

Therefore, the sum of the solutions is

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{b}{a} & =-\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186082954 :question/problem "Consider the quadratic equation

$$

$$

Therefore, the product of the solutions is

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083389 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-94608b8e-9dc6-5162-993f-c6b1291dcd79"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186082955 :question/problem "The quadratic coefficient of a particular quadratic equation equals $8.$ The sum of the solutions equals $-11,$ and the product of the solutions equals $24.$ Find the equation." :question/worked-solution "Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
ax^2 + bx + c = 0
$$

has the solutions $x = x_1$ and $x = x_2,$ where $a\neq 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
x_1 + x_2 = -\dfrac{b}{a}.
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
x_1 \cdot x_2 = \dfrac{c}{a}.
$$

Now, let's use the given information to determine the values of $a, b,$ and $c$ in this case:

- We're told that the quadratic coefficient equals $8.$ Therefore, we have

$$
a = 8.
$$

- We're told that the sum of the roots equals $-11.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-11 & =-\frac{b}{a} \\ -11 & =-\frac{b}{8} \\ 88 & =b \\ b & =88.\end{aligned}
$$

- We're told that the product of the roots equals $24.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}24 & =\frac{c}{a} \\ 24 & =\frac{c}{8} \\ 192 & =c \\ c & =192.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our equation has coefficients

$$
a = 8, \qquad b = 88, \qquad c = 192
$$

and the equation is

$$
8x^2 +88x + 192 = 0.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-761ee71b-75fd-5326-b76e-466bf3a8a311" :question/id #uuid "761ee71b-75fd-5326-b76e-466bf3a8a311" :question/math-academy-id "q-288806" :question/problem "Consider the quadratic equation

{:db/id "question-94608b8e-9dc6-5162-993f-c6b1291dcd79" :question/id #uuid "94608b8e-9dc6-5162-993f-c6b1291dcd79" :question/math-academy-id "q-288852" :question/problem "The quadratic coefficient of a particular quadratic equation equals $1.$ The sum of the solutions equals $4,$ and the product of the solutions equals $-45.$ Find the equation.

The equation is

$=0.$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0
$$

has the solutions $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ where $a\ne 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}.
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{c}{a}.
$$

Now, let's use the given information to determine the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ in this case:

- We're told that the quadratic coefficient equals $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
a=1.
$$

- We're told that the sum of the roots equals $4.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =-\frac{b}{a} \\ 4 & =-\frac{b}{1} \\ -4 & =b \\ b & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

- We're told that the product of the roots equals $-45.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-45 & =\frac{c}{a} \\ -45 & =\frac{c}{1} \\ c & =-45.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our equation has coefficients

$$
a=1,\,b=-4,\,c=-45
$$

and the equation is

$$
{x}^{2}-4x-45=0.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9a9e0ce5-acf2-5904-8c29-8541f7ebb7d6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9a9e0ce5-acf2-5904-8c29-8541f7ebb7d6" :answer-field/id #uuid "9a9e0ce5-acf2-5904-8c29-8541f7ebb7d6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-56ac2974-c463-588f-8d30-1dff0622193c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-56ac2974-c463-588f-8d30-1dff0622193c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-56ac2974-c463-588f-8d30-1dff0622193c" :answer/id #uuid "56ac2974-c463-588f-8d30-1dff0622193c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x^2-4x-45" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186084468 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the sum and the product of the solutions of the following quadratic equation:

$$
2x^2 - 160x - 6\,882 = 0
$$

One way is to find the roots and then compute their sum and product. However, this method might be cumbersome because some of the coefficients of our quadratic equation are large.

An alternative method is to use **Vieta's formulas.** Vieta's formulas state that, for a quadratic equation of the form

$$
ax^2+bx+c=0
$$

with $a \neq 0$ and two solutions $x=x_1$ and $x=x_2,$ the sum of these solutions is

$$
x_1 + x_2 = -\dfrac{b}{a},
$$

and the product of these solutions is

$$
x_1\cdot x_2 = \dfrac{c}{a}.
$$

We'll explain how these formulas are derived at the end of the lesson." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186084408 :tutorial/content "Let's find the sum and product of the solutions of our equation 

$$
2x^2 - 160x - 6\,882 = 0.
$$

In this case, we have 

$$
a=2,\qquad b=-160,\qquad c=-6\,882.
$$

Applying Vieta's formulas, we get the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =-\frac{b}{a} \\  & =-\frac{(-160)}{2} \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2} & =\frac{c}{a} \\  & =\frac{(-6\,882)}{2} \\  & =-3\,441.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's check our results. First, note that the equation can be factored as

$$
2(x+31)(x-111) = 0.
$$

Therefore, by the zero-product rule, the solutions to this equation are

$$
x_1 = -31, \qquad x_2 = 111.
$$

 

The sum of the solutions is

$$
x_1 + x_2 = -31 + 111 = 80\quad{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

and the product of the solutions is

$$
x_1\cdot x_2 = -31 \cdot 111 = -3\,441. \quad{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186084469 :tutorial/content "We'll now derive Vieta's formulas for the sum and product of the solutions of a quadratic equation.

Consider the quadratic equation 

$$
ax^2+bx+c=0
$$

with solutions $x_1$ and $x_2.$ 

According to a mathematical theorem known as the fundamental theorem of algebra, the left-hand side of our quadratic equation can *always* be factored as 

$$
ax^2+bx+c = a(x-x_1)(x-x_2).
$$

 

You'll learn more about the fundamental theorem of algebra in future lessons.

Expanding the parentheses on the right-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}) & =a({x}^{2}-{x}_{1}x-{x}_{2}x+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}) \\  & =a({x}^{2}-({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})x+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}) \\  & =a{x}^{2}-a({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})x+a{x}_{1}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is identical to the original equation, we have

$$
ax^2+bx+c = ax^2 - a(x_1 + x_2) x + ax_1x_2
$$

which is true for all values of $x.$

Since $a\neq 0,$ dividing both sides by $a,$ we obtain 

$$
x^2+{\color{blue}\dfrac{b}{a}}x+{\color{red}\dfrac{c}{a}} = x^2 \:{\color{blue}- \:(x_1+x_2)}x + {\color{red}x_1 x_2}.
$$

Since this equation is true for all values of $x,$ we can extract Vieta's formulas by equating the coefficients of the linear and constant terms on both sides of the equation, as follows:

- Equating the linear coefficients, we have

$$
{\color{blue}{\dfrac{b}{a}}} = \color{blue}-(x_1+x_2)
$$

which we can write as

$$
x_1 + x_2 = -\dfrac{b}{a}.
$$

- Equating the constants, we have

$$
x_1 x_2 = \dfrac{c}{a}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083424 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172139 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-061b72e1-6299-5d12-b681-2985a53463e0" "question-52fe2e63-f4cc-5045-bc08-fddd99b9edf2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-061b72e1-6299-5d12-b681-2985a53463e0" :question/id #uuid "061b72e1-6299-5d12-b681-2985a53463e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-26032" :question/problem "![](images/12/120d58ea1e9174a4304007c89b5de1c2f12b1312b89091d30a8b7929d6288092.png)

"36a65a87-c8d0-5bbf-adbe-0789f4e08164" :question/math-academy-id "q-336500" :question/problem "A syrup mixing tank at a bottling plant can hold up to $220\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of syrup solution with $24\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved sugar. A more concentrated sugar solution with concentration $0.7\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.7\,\text{lb/gal}$ of sugar enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.7\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.7\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =8.4\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $12\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $8\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=120+12t-8t=4(30+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(8\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{8Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =8.4-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=8.4.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 8.4 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =8.4(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =8.4(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 8.4(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =8.4\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2.8(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $24\,\text{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=24,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =24 \\ 2.8(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =24 \\ 84+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =24 \\ \frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =-60 \\ C & =-60(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2.8(30+t)-\frac{60(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =2.8(30+t)-60{(\frac{30}{30+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $220\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=220$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =220 \\ 120+12{t}_{o}-8{t}_{o} & =220 \\ 120+4{t}_{o} & =220 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =100 \\ {t}_{o} & =25\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(25) & =2.8(30+25)-60{(\frac{30}{30+25})}^{2} \\  & =154-60{(\frac{30}{55})}^{2} \\  & ≈136.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-464a658d-9140-58a9-ae22-53b8f7f33f64"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-336508" :question/problem "A wastewater treatment tank at a chemical plant can hold up to $180\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of wastewater with $40\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved contaminant. A more concentrated wastewater stream with concentration $1.25\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $1.25\,\text{lb/gal}$ of contaminant enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.25\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.25\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =15\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $12\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $8\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=120+12t-8t=4(30+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(8\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{8Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =15-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=15.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 15 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =15(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =15(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 15(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =15\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =5(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $40\,\text{lb}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=40,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =40 \\ 5(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =40 \\ 150+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =40 \\ \frac{C}{{30}^{2}} & =-110 \\ C & =-110(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =5(30+t)-\frac{110(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =5(30+t)-110{(\frac{30}{30+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 120+12{t}_{o}-8{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 120+4{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =60 \\ {t}_{o} & =15\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$

[:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-b6915e10-1543-50b0-a358-2c56a1366444" :question/id #uuid "b6915e10-1543-50b0-a358-2c56a1366444" :question/math-academy-id "q-336744" :question/problem "A fermentation tank initially holds $180\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $5\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved nutrient.
A solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved nutrient is pumped into the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min}.$ If the amount of nutrient $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins is given by

$$
Q(t)=\alpha \,(1-\frac{t}{18})+\beta {(1-\frac{t}{18})}^{3}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants, what is the value of $\alpha -\beta ?$" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which minerals enter the tank minus the rate at which minerals leave the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which minerals enter the tank.

First, note that a water solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of minerals enters the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *minerals* enter the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.8\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which minerals exit the tank.

To find the rate at which minerals leave the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $180\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $20\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $30\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
180+20t-30t=(180-10t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of minerals in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{180-10t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min},$ *minerals* leave at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(30\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{180-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{180-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{30Q}{180-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3Q}{18-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.8-\frac{3Q}{18-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{18-t}Q=0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 3/(18-t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|18-t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(18-t)^{-3}} \\  & =(18-t)^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(18-t)^{-3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(18-t)^{-3}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{18-t}Q) & =(18-t)^{-3}\cdot 0.8 \\ (18-t)^{-3}\frac{dQ}{dt}+3(18-t)^{-4}Q & =0.8(18-t)^{-3} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(18-t)^{-3}) & =0.8(18-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(18-t)^{-3})\,dt & =\int 0.8(18-t)^{-3}\,dt \\ Q(18-t)^{-3} & =0.8\cdot \frac{1}{2}(18-t)^{-2}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.4(18-t)+C(18-t)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $5\,\text{kg}$ of minerals. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=5,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =5 \\ C(18-0)^{3}+0.4(18-0) & =5 \\ C(18)^{3}+7.2 & =5 \\ C & =-\frac{2.2}{{18}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.4(18-t)-\frac{2.2}{{18}^{3}}(18-t)^{3} \\  & =0.4\cdot 18\,(\frac{18-t}{18})-2.2{(\frac{18-t}{18})}^{3} \\  & =7.2\,(1-\frac{t}{18})-2.2{(1-\frac{t}{18})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have $\alpha =7.2,\beta =-2.2,$ and

$$
\alpha -\beta =7.2-(-2.2)=9.4.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-889a0978-0193-5e72-b84c-66f0c08de47a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $f(x)=\frac{2{x}^{3}}{x(x-3)^{3}}.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{3}}{x(x-3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot {x}^{2}}{x(x-3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\cancel{x}\cdot {x}^{2}}{\cancel{x}(x-3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}}{(x-3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
(x-3)^{3}=0
$$

This gives the solution $x=3.$ Therefore, $x=3$ is the only vertical asymptote." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x-1}{(x-1)({x}^{2}-x+1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x-1}}{\cancel{(x-1)}({x}^{2}-x+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}-x+1=0
$$

The last equation does not have any real solutions because the discriminant $D$ is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(-1)^{2}-4(1)(1) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8422c58a-bb72-5552-8ac2-10a4a7678ba9"] :db/ensure $$
f(x)=\frac{3}{4}(2x-{x}^{2}),\,0\le x\le 2.
$$

Calculate $\text{E}[{X}^{3}].$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5{x}^{9/5}}{9}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5{x}^{9/5}}{9})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{5}{9}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{9/5})+0 & = \\ \frac{5}{9}\cdot \frac{9}{5}{x}^{9/5-1} & = \\ {x}^{4/5}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fa476148-4520-535e-8de8-c555998b437f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "1d37bcc4-0c9f-508d-8122-95d6a1703d93" :question/math-academy-id "q-130018" :question/problem "Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
{∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=-5,\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=-10,
$$

find the value of 

$$
{∬}_{C\cup D}2f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

:question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-2{x}_{2}(t)+1,\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=$ {{field-1}} $,\,$
${X}_{2}(s)=\frac{3s+1}{s(s+2)}$ ." :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-2{x}_{2}(t)+1\}\end{aligned}\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=-L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+4L\{{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}+L\{1\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+1=-{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-3=-2{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{1}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\},$ and we have used the fact that $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}.$

Now, solving the second equation for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s)-3 & =-2{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+2){X}_{2}(s) & =3+\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+2){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{3s+1}{s} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{3s+1}{s(s+2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the first equation and solving for ${X}_{1}(s)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+1 & =-{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s+1){X}_{1}(s) & =4{X}_{2}(s)-1 \\ (s+1){X}_{1}(s) & =4(\frac{3s+1}{s(s+2)})-1 \\ (s+1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{4(3s+1)-s(s+2)}{s(s+2)} \\ (s+1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{12s+4-({s}^{2}+2s)}{s(s+2)} \\ (s+1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-{s}^{2}+10s+4}{s(s+2)} \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-{s}^{2}+10s+4}{s(s+2)(s+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{-{s}^{2}+10s+4}{s(s+1)(s+2)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{3s+1}{s(s+2)}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b8de0228-5ef5-53a6-b77b-949275d4025a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b8de0228-5ef5-53a6-b77b-949275d4025a" :answer-field/id #uuid "b8de0228-5ef5-53a6-b77b-949275d4025a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-69712d4c-92b7-5f9d-abcd-ca7ad46c6567" :answer-field/choices ["answer-69712d4c-92b7-5f9d-abcd-ca7ad46c6567"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-69712d4c-92b7-5f9d-abcd-ca7ad46c6567" :answer/id #uuid "69712d4c-92b7-5f9d-abcd-ca7ad46c6567" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{-s^2+10s+4}{s(s+1)(s+2)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-24075bbd-fad1-5e70-847c-3b96960e39c5" :question/id #uuid "24075bbd-fad1-5e70-847c-3b96960e39c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-333072" :question/problem "$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\},$ and we have used the fact that $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s) & =-{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{3}{s} \\ (s+1){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{3}{s} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{3}{s(s+1)}.\end{aligned}

Substituting this in the first equation and solving for ${X}_{1}(s)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2 & ={X}_{1}(s)-2{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-1){X}_{1}(s) & =-2-2{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-1){X}_{1}(s) & =-2-2(\frac{3}{s(s+1)}) \\ (s-1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2s(s+1)-6}{s(s+1)} \\ (s-1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2({s}^{2}+s)-6}{s(s+1)} \\ (s-1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2{s}^{2}-2s-6}{s(s+1)} \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2{s}^{2}-2s-6}{s(s+1)(s-1)}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the solution of the new system in terms of parameter $s$ is

{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Notice that the roots of the parabola are given. They are

If the coordinates of the vertex are $(h,k),$ then by the average of the roots formula, $h$ is simply the average of the two roots. Therefore, we have

Therefore, we can find the axis of symmetry of a parabola by finding the roots and then taking their average value. 

So, if the roots are $x_1$ and $x_2,$ the **average of the roots formula** tells us that the axis of symmetry of the parabola is

$$
x = \dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}.
$$

For example, let's consider the parabola 

$$
y=(x+2)(x-4).
$$

We have the roots $x_1=-2$ and $x_2=4.$ Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{-2+4}{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=(x+2)(x-4)$ is $x=1,$ as shown below.

![](images/ec/ec08bc1ba75082ac98bb6559b6c0ef8119fbf245f3c266710ce8c6a569fa8a02.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186111821 :tutorial/content "![](images/b2/b27906f92121928be444d3b7f616becbcc7a849e1313ef50accd8c8bfd718bfb.png)

If we know two points on a parabola with *identical* $y$-values, we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking an average of the two $x$-values. 

For example, consider the parabola $y=f(x)$ above. Notice that the values of $f(x)$ at the points $x=-3$ and $x=5$ are equal.

$$
f(-3) = f(5) = 3
$$

Therefore, the parabola's axis of symmetry must be equidistant from the lines $x=-3$ and $x=5.$ We can find this by taking the average of these two values.

If the parabola's vertex is $(h,k),$ then we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =\frac{-3+5}{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $h=1$ is the $x$-coordinate of the vertex, and the axis of symmetry of the parabola is $x=1.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110824 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186171309 :answer-field/choices 17592186171312] [:db/retract 17592186171309 :answer-field/choices 17592186171313] [:db/retract 17592186171309 :answer-field/choices 17592186171314] [:db/retract 17592186171309 :answer-field/choices 17592186171310] [:db/retract 17592186171309 :answer-field/choices 17592186171311] {:db/id 17592186172614 :question/problem "$$

A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]

Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=5.$ Computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d6527b4b-120d-5aff-a1f0-c36c16a9c694"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
