$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4a313e99-6bb3-5fac-9942-cc34685e8d8e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186513010}} {:db/id 17592186513001 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229683 :question/answer-fields - We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$

$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector.

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}].

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}(-s+t+1){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-t}-t{e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cef7ab47-7ef6-5ce5-94ff-fd249257c533" :step/next {:db/id 17592186512981}}] :activity/title "Solving Inhomogeneous Systems of ODEs Using Matrix Methods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186512086} {:db/id 17592186046644} {:db/id 17592186513018 :step/content {:db/id 17592186512945 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2ce80ed6-c2fb-573a-bcb7-17c24ee2cd02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-e^{-t}" :db/id 17592186512202}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186512202} :answer-field/id #uuid "7d8ad94d-1b6b-50f4-917b-e60fcda59e4c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186512794}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "dcde9f99-5a2a-52a5-a122-c3ef3631c507" :question/math-academy-id "q-335070" :question/problem "$$

$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

|  | $1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1c1ad14e-74e6-51e6-a61f-0245fb4cfb09" :step/next {:db/id 17592186536036}} {:db/id 17592186536026 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311584 :question/answer-fields $$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "98ff146f-1e74-5987-92d5-7e14960c7748" :step/next {:db/id 17592186536026}} {:db/id 17592186536050 :step/content {:db/id 17592186535981 :question/answer-fields $$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

$$

$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$

$$

Finally, we get

$$

\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "98ff146f-1e74-5987-92d5-7e14960c7748" :step/next {:db/id 17592186536026}} {:db/id 17592186536026 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311584 :question/answer-fields $$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ from $0$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

:knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186172099 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "629dd9d1-1c53-5a04-97bf-5799e71b9573" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux Across Other Type I and Type II Regions"}] :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle -3xy^2 , \: y+\cos x \right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0), (2,2),$ and $(-2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/aa/aa822f0b9259d6d9eb5c6f439588e70d4b9bee16b2b868fae36c7cbac72d3c3f.png)

We have that $P(x,y) = -3xy^2$ and $Q(x,y) = y+\cos x .$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) :  -y \leq x \leq y, \, 0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)[x]_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)(y-(-y))\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\cdot 2y\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-6{y}^{3}+2y)\,dy \\  & =[-6\cdot \frac{{y}^{4}}{4}+2\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =[-\frac{3{y}^{4}}{2}+{y}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =(-24+4)-0 \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172304 :question/id #uuid "5f0fa3f4-0fcf-5a8c-888e-2010c07d0c94" :question/math-academy-id "q-126814"} {:db/id 17592186172305 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨6y{x}^{2}+{e}^{y},\,3{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=2.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/f6/f6e80e3010ec7c40d3f59dbb1da4e77c985c889a720b6f954177d8ad83a01351.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=6y{x}^{2}+{e}^{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=3{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=12yx,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(12yx+6y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}(12yx+6y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6{y}^{2}x+3{y}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6{x}^{2}+3x)\,dx \\  & =(2{x}^{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2})\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =22-0 \\  & =22.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262755 :question/id #uuid "b1199c00-6bec-5b54-8e65-8c9cf313406e" :question/math-academy-id "q-127316" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172099 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "629dd9d1-1c53-5a04-97bf-5799e71b9573" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux Across Other Type I and Type II Regions"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bdeb3565-33b8-5e33-8e62-a379ccee15a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186261551} {:answer/id #uuid "d61001de-9748-5fd5-a503-22e24e85614b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186261757} {:answer/id #uuid "d6b6bc8d-1963-572f-81c7-31d894805c47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3\pi " :db/id 17592186261765} {:answer/id #uuid "ec2e40f2-95b7-5d9f-a3c0-5505414cee4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186261946} {:answer/id #uuid "fbfa1d83-7d56-5a32-8910-1d3f25e76d97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186262079}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "d61001de-9748-5fd5-a503-22e24e85614b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186261757} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee924e6b-2ed7-5385-812d-4d3eda3ed721" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186262541}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨x-\sqrt{y},\,y-\sqrt{x}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and the line $y=0$ for $0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/c4/c4dd4d03bdfcf6c3d597e2fdef8681e4f3316b3f276cb9967933b61b0dc90976.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x-\sqrt{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=y-\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore,

$$

$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dx \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2(0-(-1)) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.

$$

$$
D = \{(x,y) :  -1\leq x\leq 1, \, -3\leq y \leq 0\}
$$

$$

Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)={x}^{2}y\,i+5xy\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/26/265d27ad87a7f114bd2a32a5f48cbfedb13192abf48f9b759c4ed635e71ff144.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=5xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =5x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+5x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(2y+5)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262728 :question/id #uuid "c8fd9f34-b5c0-5dde-8e43-965eb6f71e26" :question/math-academy-id "q-127206" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172100 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5c7e707-c978-566d-8a69-98c84c7eb53e" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25758b2a-af8a-5a90-81ab-acfe72d274c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2xy" :db/id 17592186260201} {:answer/id #uuid "66ae0255-9a5f-52f4-acb5-19660b53dbce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2xy" :db/id 17592186260769} {:answer/id #uuid "904beab1-505f-5e48-a793-2b0d5eec535a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186261129} {:answer/id #uuid "d53f3519-e121-50e5-9ddf-3dbe90831402" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6xy" :db/id 17592186261752} {:answer/id #uuid "e7611642-0621-5c4d-9835-a60ea38e0d68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186261904}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "66ae0255-9a5f-52f4-acb5-19660b53dbce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2xy" :db/id 17592186260769} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b4f3e47-9d1d-52ec-bb38-4c32ab7f1c29" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186262369}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field

$$

$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/98/98d7da0c7cd1e1f1006c1db74ae1a1e1f198d9066df6585745ee36548f0b8d96.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y+2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2xy.\end{aligned}

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$

:knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux Across Rectangles"}] :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle \sin(\pi y) - x , \: \cos(\pi x) + 2xy \right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(0,-1), (2,-1), (2,1),$ and $(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/2f/2f3374de4a29c62587a79f6286dfe788e64c37e09e9d9b83b3a67b4dac10dc21.png)

We have that $P(x,y) = \sin(\pi y) - x$ and $Q(x,y) = \cos(\pi x) + 2xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) :  0 \leq x \leq 2, \, -1 \leq y \leq 1 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}-x)\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({2}^{2}-2)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2\,dy \\  & =2y\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2(1)-2(-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186520745} {:db/id 17592186172306 :question/id #uuid "e4e547a4-3c18-52fb-b4b9-408da110d4a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-126820"} {:db/id 17592186172307 :question/id #uuid We have that $P(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{y}+x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-6{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(1-6{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-2{x}^{3}y)\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(2-2(2)^{3}y)-0]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2-16y)\,dy \\  & =[2y-8{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(2(1)-8(1)^{2})-0 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{2}+8x{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{x}+2{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=8{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =4y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(8{y}^{3}+4y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(8{y}^{3}+4y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8{y}^{3}+4y)\,x\,{|}_{-1}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8{y}^{3}+4y)\cdot 1\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8{y}^{3}+4y)\,dy \\  & =[2{y}^{4}+2{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(2(1)^{4}+2(1)^{2})-0 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

"b533c8b3-90f2-54ee-ae35-a98929d6ba6e" :step/math-academy-id 35837 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173009}} {:db/id 17592186173012 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic "fluxes" (divergences) of $\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$

![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)

    

Recall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\mathbf F$ at a point is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

If we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A.
$$

This expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.

The macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s
$$

Equating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have

$$
\iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y} \right)\textrm d A = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \mathbf n \, \textrm d s.
$$

The flux form of Green's theorem can be summarized in a single picture, as follows:

![](images/0f/0f8ba4b7e853e3b59e8677b0954c3cfae1b9c482750e13a742bd4d45eda8005d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9016229b-93aa-58fc-857c-2a2d3f337ca4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5862 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind Green's Theorem in Flux Form"} :step/id #uuid "e5c29654-0b83-51e0-a3d0-c6fbf08c8f2d" :step/math-academy-id 35877 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173010}} {:db/id 17592186173013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173208 :tutorial/content "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. Even more, Green's theorem can also be used to simplify flux calculations!

To see how, we first recall that the flux of $\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\mathbf j$ across $C$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s= \oint\limits_C P\, \textrm{d}y -Q\, \textrm{d}x
$$

where $C$ is closed and $\mathbf n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Now, let's set $M= -Q$ and $N=P$. Then, by the circulation form of Green's theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x & ={∮}_{C}N\,\text{d}y+M\,\text{d}x \\  & ={∮}_{C}M\,\text{d}x+N\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂N}{∂x}-\frac{∂M}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}-(-\frac{∂Q}{∂y}))\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we've obtained the **Green's theorem in flux form**, which we restate below:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} +\dfrac{\partial  Q}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A
$$

Now, recall that the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F =  \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

Therefore, we can also write Green's theorem in flux form as

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form allows us to convert a flux line integral into an equivalent double integral." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f3b4b70-8b58-53d1-bc8d-a42daddfab4d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5868 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "528120c2-edf7-5b3d-a8d3-0b481b460d90" :step/math-academy-id 35900 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173012}}] :activity/title "Green's Theorem in Flux Form" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172181} {:db/id 17592186173013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173208 :tutorial/content "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. through $C$ as a repeated integral." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/26/265d27ad87a7f114bd2a32a5f48cbfedb13192abf48f9b759c4ed635e71ff144.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=5xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =5x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
F(x,y)=⟨x+\sqrt{y},\,y+\sqrt{x}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and the line $y=0$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e5/e570374b37c116e32c3a7762b8cf09a28bdbb3e06b5e67e25837902a89bcd264.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x+\sqrt{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=y+\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{cos}⁡x\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dx \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ec17ec80-3152-54be-96ed-dd7762345db6"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4a2f6f5b-f063-50fd-a445-e5206861484d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int :knowledge-point/id #uuid "03456ac4-5798-56cc-8c14-0a645b2e232e" :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Sum of the Roots of a Quadratic Equation"}] :question/problem "Consider the quadratic equation
$8x^2 + 5x - 12 = 0$.
**Without** solving the equation, determine the sum of its solutions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
ax^2 + bx + c = 0
$$

has the solutions $x = x_1$ and $x = x_2$, where

$$
a\neq 0
$$

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by
$x_1 + x_2 = -\dfrac{b}{a}$.
- The product of the solutions is given by
$x_1 \cdot x_2 = \dfrac{c}{a}$.

For the given quadratic equation, we have

$$
a = 8, \qquad b = 5, \qquad c = -12
$$

Therefore, the sum of the solutions is

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\frac{b}{a} &= -\frac{5}{8}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048938} {:db/id 17592186049077} {:db/id 17592186083647 :question/id #uuid "3a148b41-3796-598a-9910-94ca2245fb46" :question/math-academy-id "q-288777"} {:db/id 17592186083648 :question/id #uuid "815e8b4f-7914-5a73-ae67-1c267a95c9db" :question/math-academy-id "q-288811"} {:db/id 17592186233741 :question/id #uuid "0f4b1e55-33db-5937-89ea-ee62b50a7a5d" :question/math-academy-id "q-288778"} {:db/id 17592186233742 :question/id #uuid "2b88b5a5-162d-5e5e-ac66-e7153ed0510e" :question/math-academy-id "q-288810" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186083387 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "03456ac4-5798-56cc-8c14-0a645b2e232e" :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Sum of the Roots of a Quadratic Equation"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the quadratic equation

$$
{x}^{2}+172x-15\,300=0.
$$

**Without** solving the equation, determine the sum of its solutions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0
$$

has the solutions $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ where $a\ne 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}.
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{c}{a}.
$$

For the given quadratic equation, we have

$$
a=1,\,b=172,\,c=-15\,300.
$$

Therefore, the sum of the solutions is

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{b}{a} & =-\frac{172}{1}=-172.\end{aligned}

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186084368 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084468 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the sum and the product of the solutions of the following quadratic equation:

$$
2x^2 - 160x - 6\,882 = 0
$$

One way is to find the roots and then compute their sum and product. However, this method might be cumbersome because some of the coefficients of our quadratic equation are large.

An alternative method is to use **Vieta's formulas.** Vieta's formulas state that, for a quadratic equation of the form

$$
ax^2+bx+c=0
$$

with

$$
a \neq 0
$$

and two solutions $x=x_1$ and $x=x_2$, the sum of these solutions is

$$
x_1 + x_2 = -\dfrac{b}{a}
$$

and the product of these solutions is

$$
x_1\cdot x_2 = \dfrac{c}{a}
$$

We'll explain how these formulas are derived at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "a1bacc29-6f0e-5c99-aab3-8a77154a17d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4442 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5898a8e1-42dd-5ff7-9540-b7ded63e6b27" :step/math-academy-id 476832 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084369}} {:db/id 17592186084369 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084408 :tutorial/content "Let's find the sum and product of the solutions of our equation

$$
2x^2 - 160x - 6\,882 = 0
$$

In this case, we have

$$
a=2,\qquad b=-160,\qquad c=-6\,882
$$

Applying Vieta's formulas, we get the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by
$x_{1} + x_{2}|=-\frac{b}{a}; = - ((-160))/(2); = 80$.
- The product of the solutions is given by
$x_{1} \cdot x_{2}|= \frac{c}{a}; = ((-6882))/(2); =-3441$.

Finally, let's check our results. First, note that the equation can be factored as

$$
2(x+31)(x-111) = 0
$$

Therefore, by the zero-product rule, the solutions to this equation are

$$
x_1 = -31, \qquad x_2 = 111
$$

The sum of the solutions is

$$
x_1 + x_2 = -31 + 111 = 80\quad{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

and the product of the solutions is

$$
x_1\cdot x_2 = -31 \cdot 111 = -3\,441. \quad{\color{green}\checkmark}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c978ee52-e1ec-57b7-8779-be1d9aaa0ea9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13437 :tutorial/title "Applying Vieta's Formulas"} :step/id #uuid "cd57ada6-8f57-54fc-9dad-877823f35b12" - Equating the constants, we have

bisector of the segment joining the two points.

For example, suppose that the line $l$ reflects the point $A$ onto $A'$ below. How can we find the equation of $l?$

![](images/79/79ddc15badc704a9c9860207a5156c3a0505ab626572581bcf3146976338a015.png)

The line $l$ is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment $\overline{AA'}.$ So, the line of reflection is $y=-1.$

![](images/aa/aa240e562acf388bdf05751e680e917bc8465bad34300334f6b423df46a7d1f3.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "8464dac5-c554-50b1-94c2-4e8df122e9fb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2363 :tutorial/title "Identifying the Line of Reflection"} :step/id #uuid "0b163811-1b76-5f40-981e-e52237413897" :step/math-academy-id 10216 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173106}} {:db/id 17592186173104 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173142 :tutorial/content "We can reflect an object in any line. Consider the diagram below. The two polygons are the mirror images of each other in the line $l.$

![](images/1e/1e4dfb2939916df5d5018320819f14fcec261a1e77c171b551e9868a8c3bebc8.png)

If we want to reflect the quadrilateral $ABCD$ below in the line $l,$ we can reflect each vertex separately and then draw the segments between the resulting corresponding vertices.

![](images/a4/a47c41b41ecae2bc4c281e1b90c843ae68fa907a0d2ff49c48454fd80e2977c7.png)

Let's start by reflecting the point $A.$ To do this, we need to plot a new point $A'$ on the opposite side of $l$ at an equal distance away from $l$ as the original point $A.$

The original point $A$ is $4$ units to the left of $l,$ so we need to plot the new point $A'$ at a distance of $4$ units to the right of $l.$

![](images/33/33bb82c9d0f20df13f46060b9aec21e8c4d1231766926c47b7718bf58e1c5e32.png)

Now let's reflect other vertices of the quadrilateral in the same way:

![](images/00/00ec763ccce462effa024486a6ff09a98b549c61179de18bb850470e835a7627.png)

Finally, we draw segments between the reflected vertices.

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "A processing tank initially holds $420\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $10\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved preservative.
A feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the preservative is pumped into the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of preservative in the tank $15$ minutes after pumping begins." :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of preservative in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which preservative enters the tank minus the rate at which preservative leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which preservative enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the preservative enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *preservative* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.9\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which preservative exits the tank.

To find the rate at which preservative leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $420\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $18\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $12\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
420+18t-12t=(420+6t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of preservative in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min},$ *preservative* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{70+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.9-\frac{2Q}{70+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q=0.9.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(70+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|70+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =(70+t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(70+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(70+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q) & =(70+t)^{2}\cdot 0.9 \\ (70+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(70+t)Q & =0.9(70+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2}) & =0.9(70+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 0.9(70+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(70+t)^{2} & =0.9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(70+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.3(70+t)+\frac{C}{(70+t)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $10\,\text{kg}$ of preservative. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ 0.3(70+0)+\frac{C}{(70+0)^{2}} & =10 \\ 21+\frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =10 \\ \frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =-11 \\ C & =-11(70)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.3(70+t)-\frac{11(70)^{2}}{(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =0.3(70+t)-11{(\frac{70}{70+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of preservative in the tank $15$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(15) & =0.3(70+15)-11{(\frac{70}{70+15})}^{2} \\  & =25.5-11{(\frac{70}{85})}^{2} \\  & ≈18.04\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "A dye mixing tank at a textile factory can hold up to $180\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of solution with $20\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved dye. A more concentrated dye solution with concentration $0.6\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dye enters the tank minus the rate at which dye leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dye enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.6\,\text{lb/gal}$ of dye enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dye* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =9\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

To find the rate at which dye leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=100+15t-10t=5(20+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{20+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{20+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q=9.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(20+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|20+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(20+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(20+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q) & =(20+t)^{2}\cdot 9 \\ (20+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(20+t)Q & =9(20+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2}) & =9(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 9(20+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(20+t)^{2} & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(20+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3(20+t)+\frac{C}{(20+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $20\,\text{lb}$ of dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =20 \\ 3(20+0)+\frac{C}{(20+0)^{2}} & =20 \\ 60+\frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =20 \\ \frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =-40 \\ C & =-40(20)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(20+t)-\frac{40(20)^{2}}{(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(20+t)-40{(\frac{20}{20+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 100+15{t}_{o}-10{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 100+5{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =80 \\ {t}_{o} & =16\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(16) & =3(20+16)-40{(\frac{20}{20+16})}^{2} \\  & =108-40{(\frac{20}{36})}^{2} \\  & ≈95.7\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186385215 :question/id #uuid "9d3bb996-2c5a-57e9-940a-6b48f2e05670" :question/math-academy-id "q-336502"} {:db/id 17592186502072 :question/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 6700} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186230082 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230205 :tutorial/content "In the previous lesson, we focused on dilution problems in which the incoming solution contained none of the substance being modeled. In those cases, the rate at which the substance entered the container was zero.

In many practical situations, however, the incoming solution *does* contain some amount of the substance. When this happens,

- the rate of entry is no longer zero, and

- the resulting differential equation takes the form of a first-order linear differential equation.

For example, suppose a storage tank initially holds $650\,\textrm{L}$ of water containing $1\,300\,\textrm{g}$ of dissolved chlorine.

- A solution containing $20\,\textrm{g/L}$ of dissolved chlorine is pumped into the tank at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

- At the same time, the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

To construct the model for the amount of chlorine $Q$ in the tank, we compare the rates of chlorine entering and leaving. The derivative 
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}$
describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which chlorine enters the tank minus the rate at which chlorine leaves the tank.

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}}}
$$

We compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine enters the tank.

The rate of chlorine entering is the concentration times the flow rate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =100\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine exits the tank.

Since the volume remains constant at $650\,\textrm{L},$ the concentration in the tank is $\dfrac{Q}{650}\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{L}}.$ So, the rate of chlorine exiting is

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{Q}{130}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The net rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_\text{in} - Q'_\text{out}$ is the difference between the rate in and the rate out. Combining this with the initial condition $Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g},$ we can state the complete initial value problem:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = 100 - \dfrac{1}{130}Q
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{1}{130}Q = 100, \quad Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc8b0fc6-c25c-50f5-adbd-028adf7c6698" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14578 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "70852def-fb14-50cc-b88d-6fe2af2343bf" \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{1}{130}Q = 100, \quad Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc8b0fc6-c25c-50f5-adbd-028adf7c6698" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14578 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "70852def-fb14-50cc-b88d-6fe2af2343bf" :step/math-academy-id 601750 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230083}} {:db/id 17592186230205 :tutorial/content "In the previous lesson, we focused on dilution problems in which the incoming solution contained none of the substance being modeled. In those cases, the rate at which the substance entered the container was zero.

In many practical situations, however, the incoming solution *does* contain some amount of the substance. When this happens,

- the rate of entry is no longer zero, and

- the resulting differential equation takes the form of a first-order linear differential equation.

For example, suppose a storage tank initially holds $650\,\textrm{L}$ of water containing $1\,300\,\textrm{g}$ of dissolved chlorine.

- A solution containing $20\,\textrm{g/L}$ of dissolved chlorine is pumped into the tank at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

- At the same time, the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $5\,\textrm{L/min}.$

To construct the model for the amount of chlorine $Q$ in the tank, we compare the rates of chlorine entering and leaving. The derivative 
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}$
describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which chlorine enters the tank minus the rate at which chlorine leaves the tank.

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\textrm{out}}}
$$

We compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine enters the tank.

The rate of chlorine entering is the concentration times the flow rate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =100\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine exits the tank.

Since the volume remains constant at $650\,\textrm{L},$ the concentration in the tank is $\dfrac{Q}{650}\,\dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{L}}.$ So, the rate of chlorine exiting is

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{650}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{Q}{130}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The net rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_\text{in} - Q'_\text{out}$ is the difference between the rate in and the rate out. Combining this with the initial condition $Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g},$ we can state the complete initial value problem:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = 100 - \dfrac{1}{130}Q
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{1}{130}Q = 100, \quad Q(0) = 1\,300\,\textrm{g}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc8b0fc6-c25c-50f5-adbd-028adf7c6698" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14578 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186230083 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229181 close but never touches.

For example, let's consider the rational function 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{(x-2)(x+2)}.
$$

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

![](images/79/79e02370d60aec1e1e7f9e21dafbb876ea1f9b9b2de2b3d2b8b6ba14ffabfe3d.png)

The two dotted lines $x=2$ and $x=-2$ are the vertical asymptotes of the function. The function gets closer and closer to these lines but never touches them.

But how can we calculate the vertical asymptotes of a function without using a graph?

In general, we can find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function using the following procedure:

1\. Factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors.

2\. Set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x .$

In our case, the function is already factored, and there are no common factors in the numerator and denominator. So, to find the vertical asymptotes, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x{:}$

$$
(x-2)(x+2) = 0
$$

The solutions to this equation are $x=2$ and $x=-2.$  Therefore, the equations of the vertical asymptotes are $x=-2$ and $x=2.$ This matches up with what we saw in the graph." :tutorial/id #uuid \text{Null}(A)=\{{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\,|\,{x}_{1}\in R\}

we conclude that 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))=1\ne 0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Since $\text{dim(Null}(A))\ne 0,$ then according to the invertible matrix theorem, the matrix $A$ can't be invertible.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is not invertible, then by the invertible matrix theorem, we must have $\text{rank}(A)\ne 5.$

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=n=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately. 

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{Null}(A)$ has no basis.* $\,\times $ 

Since $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ we have $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}$ which, in turn, means that $\text{Null}(A)$ must have a basis.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $A$ is **not** invertible.* $\,✓$

Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ we must have that $A$ is **not** invertible.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.* $\,\times $

Since $A$ is not invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{n},$ which means that not all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.

$(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{x}{xy} \\  & =\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is defined only for

$$
\begin{aligned}y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186436747 :question/id #uuid "5c311fab-0276-5890-a0ca-a5fc54209d6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-132642"} {:db/id 17592186436748 :question/id #uuid At points in the domain of $f,$ we can compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{y}{(x+y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y}{x(x+y)} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{x+y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. The function is defined at $(1,1),$ since

$$
f(1,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{1+1})=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}),
$$

and both partial derivatives are defined there:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =\frac{1}{1(1+1)}=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =-\frac{1}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. At $(0,1),$

$$
\frac{x}{x+y}=\frac{0}{0+1}=0,
$$

so

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined. Therefore, ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is not defined.

- Statement III is false for the same reason. Since $f$ is not defined at $(0,1),$ the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is not defined. The simplified expression $-\frac{1}{x+y}$ cannot be used to define the partial derivative at a point outside the domain of $f.$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${f}_{y}(1,1,1)$ is defined

- **II.** ${f}_{z}(0,1,2)$ is defined

- **III.** The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(0,1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+y-z}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1,1)=\sqrt{2\cdot 1+1-1}=\sqrt{2},
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1,1) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\cdot 1+1-1}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,2)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(0,1,2)=\sqrt{2\cdot 0+1-2}=\sqrt{-1},
$$

which is undefined since the number under the radical is negative.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 0+1-1}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I only'."} {:db/id 17592186409557 :question/id #uuid "0a3b6388-98bd-5083-8d1c-f60a05890b23" :question/math-academy-id "q-132726" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e148fac7-727b-55d9-ba67-0a9fc7a276e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453368} {:answer/id #uuid "6c6ec723-5cd2-5173-b8f1-1778f583295d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453369}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453369} :answer-field/id #uuid "4e8e1392-18d1-56b3-b0f5-ff3dd861687a" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454434} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a536093-cb71-5d44-a52f-8e05b4b9f74a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453370} {:answer/id #uuid "cc2d5ab2-a228-5241-aef5-decbffea282c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453371}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453371} :answer-field/id #uuid "deacc4af-75f1-5a94-a0d0-5d1ad4ac3ea8" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454435} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "80b4f556-0cc0-5fc7-9fac-56ff9260d6c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453372} {:answer/id #uuid "cbd91732-9818-5742-9c5d-ea668d6dbe0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453373}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453373} :answer-field/id #uuid "7f7af479-38a3-58de-bca6-c137a88e2790" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454436}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,\sqrt{3})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} {:db/id 17592186409558 :question/id #uuid "538fdcf0-8dcd-525c-becd-0317742dbf1a" :question/math-academy-id "q-72010" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "899f43e4-fc9a-5506-b84d-a25c2d9eb6f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453928} {:answer/id #uuid "ec4690b4-12f7-5ffd-a0f0-d137fa95703c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453929}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453928} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ccf0ae7-dc64-51f0-892e-8d88c6910e82" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454714} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "376cf739-f8d8-5cb0-91a0-52b41ea250c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453930} {:answer/id #uuid "ffcc07c3-7704-591c-aebf-ff0249e9dd10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453931}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453931} :answer-field/id #uuid "72f29120-e8c2-52fc-abd7-8386d5f878c4" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454715} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fc77c615-3280-58d4-a19d-18282a3f7486" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453932} {:answer/id #uuid "8cfc9ce4-4706-5c6b-8f71-059b43d404d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453933}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453932} :answer-field/id #uuid "a7c89136-ff34-5898-9f58-5a98f17bcfb1" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454716}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,-1)$

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(1,-1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)}}=-{e}^{\sqrt{-1}}
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}={e}^{1}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=-\frac{e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot \frac{{e}^{\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}}{2\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}=\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II  only'."} {:db/id 17592186436752 :question/id #uuid "efd3e6cc-b29d-5cd4-ba97-6a3820c7c7c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-132672"} {:db/id 17592186493937 :question/id #uuid "970e7795-a408-5210-80aa-25f375509b0b" :question/math-academy-id "q-65263" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "084ca7fb-683b-515d-bd79-6b47f18630b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186493404} {:answer/id #uuid "1352f5a0-9197-5682-a147-c4c731774502" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186493425} {:answer/id #uuid "6a0ef88e-c7ac-5cdc-ae0e-1efc196b01b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186493549} {:answer/id #uuid "82a72c3b-2c62-5d09-a02a-39b20b9aa673" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186493599} {:answer/id #uuid "d3bc4946-5ae0-59ab-8397-c509f69337df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186493726}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493549} :answer-field/id #uuid "8c27c81b-25fa-5185-a05b-37e0f78454cf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493847}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}?$

III. ${f}_{z}(1,1,0)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{yz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{yz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xz}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xz{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{xy}{2\sqrt{xyz}} \\  & =\frac{xy{e}^{\sqrt{xyz}}}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1)(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(1)(-1)(-1)}}=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(-1,1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(-1,1,1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(1)(1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{-1}},
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into ${f}_{z}$, we get

$$
{f}_{z}(1,1,0)=\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}}{2\sqrt{1\cdot 1\cdot 0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.
