:question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{xz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $-1\le xyz\le 1.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}}$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(xyz)^{2} & >0 \\ (xyz)^{2} & <1 \\ |xyz| & <1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives $-1<xyz<1.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186125193 :question/id #uuid "0790aa49-4020-5e37-b9fd-2a18a4aa638d" :question/math-academy-id "q-65252"} {:db/id 17592186268902 :question/id #uuid "a66c3ca8-3dc1-5636-a0ae-fd45747b8bcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-132649"} {:db/id 17592186268903 :question/id #uuid "f03ff15b-864a-54f0-95c4-85eaad4622ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-132650" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e9af209-8790-5051-b760-8a2b7ab58c1e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1\}" :db/id 17592186493443} {:answer/id #uuid "2ae2e06a-4a60-5d0a-89f7-a1206ad8886c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186493462} {:answer/id #uuid "4da31340-f280-5ea2-b625-950af86420b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1\}" :db/id 17592186493517} {:answer/id #uuid "ee12a67f-64f9-5a94-956a-3d8cefbc2906" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0,\,z>0\}" :db/id 17592186493770} {:answer/id #uuid "f1099e4d-5739-5e2b-abdc-97a47dbd0d32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186493778}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493462} :answer-field/id #uuid "544bcd11-f607-53b0-99d1-1273ed387e89" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268559}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)},\,\frac{∂g}{∂z}=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{z}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2x}{z({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1\ne 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={D}_{{g}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{z}(x,y,z)=-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1)}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} & ={D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{z}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & \,\,\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>1,\,z\ne 0\}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268904 :question/id #uuid "9c09835a-efb6-5fd7-a6fa-37a21ebe5b95" :question/math-academy-id "q-132651"} {:db/id 17592186339043 :question/id #uuid "329fb25a-c39e-587a-8c51-720f867dc9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72005" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8b4579a6-884f-5620-9c48-03f859207fbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}" :db/id 17592186337292} {:answer/id #uuid "aa211335-2ec0-5533-aaf0-0747d0111e9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ge 0}" :db/id 17592186337566} {:answer/id #uuid "ab12ccaa-59a3-5391-8885-0e57cfa9220d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<0}" :db/id 17592186337575} {:answer/id #uuid "d30b5af1-be96-52a2-983e-53d94d787930" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186337875} {:answer/id #uuid "d932ef34-432a-58eb-96dc-98456b7b3465" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0}" :db/id 17592186337921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337292} :answer-field/id #uuid "167ce942-9903-5739-b46e-634adbd1db2c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338315}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ and

$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z},

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $xyz>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$

$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\}.

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.\end{aligned}

\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{y{sin}^{2}⁡z}
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,e]\times [2,3].$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-2){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{-1}^{0}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2({x}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{0}) \\  & =2({0}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}6{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{2}6{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{y}^{3}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\cdot {2}^{3}-0 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(3{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=2+16=18.\end{aligned}

$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}

17592186045493} :db/id 17592186153880}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5},\,0<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20},$ compute $\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+\text{E}[1] \\  & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5}+\frac{4}{5}{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{10}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{5}{x}^{4})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{3}]=\frac{3}{10}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{11}{20}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{11}{10}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186157991 :question/id #uuid "eae3a531-2321-5b4a-b69a-406252623915" :question/math-academy-id "q-90279"} {:db/id 17592186427364 :question/id #uuid "63bcffd8-dbf0-5c48-8ca6-56531c05d1c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-131141" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33cb4776-7d73-5e89-be66-3abb80c22cd1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}" :db/id 17592186427291} {:answer/id #uuid "5d5bf664-a18f-566d-a4f7-3bd738b55f2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186427301} {:answer/id #uuid "74d74ac0-e401-549d-95e1-5b551db31568" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}+2" :db/id 17592186427309} {:answer/id #uuid "aa2240d8-61b4-5dec-86e4-1ecedc83ab1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186427322} {:answer/id #uuid "ce1156f5-fddd-5d6b-adf1-9732ee27312f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{e}-1" :db/id 17592186427333}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186427291} :answer-field/id #uuid "62e8ebaf-8a75-5cb6-8621-5bcf5f7ac9e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186427348}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2x},\,{e}^{-2}<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}},$ compute $\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X]=4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{{e}^{-2}}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,|}_{{e}^{-2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4{X}^{2}-2X] & =4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X] \\  & =4(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4{e}^{4}})-2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}-1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186427367 :question/id #uuid "78882664-5ca1-5d0e-9798-9cca3f283762" :question/math-academy-id "q-90451"} {:db/id 17592186427369 :question/id #uuid "8ee689ae-d309-5b9e-a1ff-6e4de3b135ae" :question/math-academy-id "q-90454"} {:db/id 17592186427370 :question/id #uuid "90065876-8b39-51cd-875c-5aa5721dc0eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-131143"} {:db/id 17592186427371 :question/id #uuid "993709fe-5242-5062-93c5-df6c430c3cdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-131152"} {:db/id 17592186434427 :question/id #uuid "cf5c8a43-29b3-589c-9d23-ef6cc2a81919" :question/math-academy-id "q-131142" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7b58a9e1-f2e5-5bab-86c3-1dc62a5bf1dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186434407} {:answer/id #uuid "83994b5b-dec3-525b-9473-71abebd50a27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186434408} {:answer/id #uuid "908f1924-a4cc-5cae-83ec-6a4c7872904f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186434410} {:answer/id #uuid "93d5d0a4-79ad-5a4d-854e-315f284a4eac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186434411} {:answer/id #uuid "a25f9bac-857f-5e6a-8fee-76b7ccf2820e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186434412}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186434408} :answer-field/id #uuid "9c9c34c2-a686-5dff-8116-1e613117e2fd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186434424}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2},\,1<x<3
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=2,$ compute $\text{E}[5X-3{X}^{2}].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[5X-3{X}^{2}]=5\text{E}[X]-3\text{E}[{X}^{2}]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\,|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=2$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{13}{3}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[5X-3{X}^{2}] & =5\text{E}[X]-3\text{E}[{X}^{2}] \\  & =5\cdot 2-3\cdot \frac{13}{3} \\  & =10-13 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186434428 :question/id #uuid "fc2748a6-b91a-5b23-b40c-5cede2d8d71d" :question/math-academy-id "q-90394"} {:db/id 17592186479144 :question/id #uuid "f6cddda8-c777-5283-b03a-3671533a782a" :question/math-academy-id "q-131153" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1cfd005b-75a8-5b0f-ba56-4a0ed93ab33a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186478604} {:answer/id #uuid "22afcee8-e19d-562c-b205-332bc6a88919" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186478613} {:answer/id #uuid "7a90c263-2858-513a-872f-0ae63784d35a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186478741} {:answer/id #uuid "edf857b5-69b2-5c68-8336-4b0f3c36ec60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186478931} {:answer/id #uuid "ff85e4b7-ab02-503c-8793-d2b775c75049" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186478958}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186478958} :answer-field/id #uuid "623ea09b-af47-50f2-9745-0713c7359869" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186478997}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}].$

$$
f(x)=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}},\,1<x<2
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}]=10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=2$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}] & =10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}] \\  & =10-4\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186508043 :question/id #uuid "0cddfc6e-37ce-5b87-9aa0-8b3fda1d2938" :question/math-academy-id "q-90392" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13ed44a6-241d-5838-9fc9-af9b6f83e61d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186507622} {:answer/id #uuid "1578c936-8ad1-508e-aa56-b4990c519451" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186507624} {:answer/id #uuid "67abf3a2-af43-5891-a4b8-887a1c46a81b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186507751} {:answer/id #uuid "7e517eaa-0474-52ae-938e-84dbfaa53de5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186507784} {:answer/id #uuid "8dda24db-7965-57a0-84c8-bf571ddd300c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}" :db/id 17592186507800}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507624} :answer-field/id #uuid "f5d3c470-c959-5590-9ddc-7ea57ee65776" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186508029}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{3}{{x}^{4}},\,x>1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{2},$ compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}+2X-1].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}+2X-1] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]+2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[1] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]+2\text{E}[X]-1\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{3}{x})|}_{1}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(3-\frac{3}{a}) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{2}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=3$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}+2X-1] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]+2\text{E}[X]-1 \\  & =3+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}-1 \\  & =3+3-1 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186508093 :question/id #uuid "b8f3b4b6-eb37-510a-a5f6-48850ac9d684" :question/math-academy-id "q-131140" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b2368f6-3f68-54b0-9d32-a27cbf3895be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}+e-2" :db/id 17592186507648} {:answer/id #uuid "b02c68e4-e61b-5654-9879-70de70a8fe6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}-2e+3" :db/id 17592186507843} {:answer/id #uuid "b269375e-588f-5e5f-9ae9-591c8a3221c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2}-e" :db/id 17592186507845} {:answer/id #uuid "bfd68903-0ef9-5e2a-88ed-3677ac3ae07b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}-e" :db/id 17592186507864} {:answer/id #uuid "c01cb739-f7ab-5ebb-8e34-daf477537efd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2}-5e+3" :db/id 17592186507865}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507864} :answer-field/id #uuid "440eb13c-81c4-5c5d-9faa-611d1e590780" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186507967}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,1<x<e
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=e-1,$ compute $\text{E}[2{X}^{2}-X].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[2{X}^{2}-X]=2\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=e-1$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2{X}^{2}-X] & =2\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}-(e-1) \\  & ={e}^{2}-1-e+1 \\  & ={e}^{2}-e.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186157394 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186156995 :question/id #uuid "292610ec-9c27-590d-b207-c76adc959d55" :question/math-academy-id "e-10528"} :knowledge-point/id Calculate $\text{E}[{X}^{4}].$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the fourth raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{4}] & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{x}^{4}\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\,{x}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({e}^{8}-1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{8}-1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186479070 :question/id #uuid "2317ff10-80a3-5747-858a-863cca47fbc9" :question/math-academy-id "q-152922" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1370ffbd-2eab-5260-a0b4-0bf5d3cdb6db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{5}" :db/id 17592186478582} {:answer/id #uuid "7f3f6cb5-53fa-5af5-81d3-830801107641" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{17}{9}" :db/id 17592186478750} {:answer/id #uuid "82d2a8f9-d415-5d71-a7d9-fe699cab072f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{21}{25}" :db/id 17592186478758} {:answer/id #uuid "bedb09af-8e03-5cb2-a39f-8ac2f91ce3a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{19}{16}" :db/id 17592186478867} {:answer/id #uuid "e89460a9-557b-5055-9a71-6a052e322419" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{6}" :db/id 17592186478921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186478867} :answer-field/id #uuid "aded51f8-58f0-5888-884c-244971621142" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186479026}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{16}\,{x}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{x}){|}_{1}^{a} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}(1-0)+{lim}_{a\to \infty }(1-\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{16}+(1-0) \\  & =\frac{19}{16}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186479115 :question/id #uuid "ac78b028-e0aa-5c92-b54a-b1ba1527a82f" :question/math-academy-id "q-152915" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "85e8f87d-a86b-5e5a-9b4c-520af1d67778" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/id 17592186478767} {:answer/id #uuid "8a5de172-0879-5846-8775-50301538400b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186478775} {:answer/id #uuid "8c404e33-978f-5492-8afd-92388f08864c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{8}" :db/id 17592186478781} {:answer/id #uuid "92a6058f-3718-55b4-83a2-afc873b42494" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{6}{5}" :db/id 17592186478797} {:answer/id #uuid "a7862d49-f18d-5362-98d3-095ce5b8964a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{13}{5}" :db/id 17592186478832}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186478832} :answer-field/id #uuid "63b35dd5-9730-5404-b881-f84b63c0e854" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186478998}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function

{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "If ${Z}_{i}∼N(0,1)$ for $1\le i\le k$ are independent normal random variables, then the sum

$$
{Z}_{1}^{2}+{Z}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{Z}_{k}^{2}
$$

follows a ${χ}^{2}(k)$ distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom.

So, in our case, we have

$$
Y={Z}_{1}^{2}+{Z}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{Z}_{50}^{2}∼{χ}^{2}(50).
$$

First, we express the given probability in the form $P(Y\ge y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le y) & =1-P(Y\ge y) \\ 0.85 & =1-P(Y\ge y) \\ P(Y\ge y) & =0.15\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we wish to find the value $y$ such that $P(Y\ge y)=0.15$ This can be found from the given table:

| $k∖p$ | $0.010$ | $0.050$ | $0.100$ | $0.150$ | $0.200$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $48$ | $\,73.683\,$ | $\,65.171\,$ | $\,60.907\,$ | $\,58.135\,$ | $\,55.993\,$ |
| $49$ | $\,74.919\,$ | $\,66.339\,$ | $\,62.038\,$ | $\,59.241\,$ | $\,57.079\,$ |
| $50$ | $\,76.154\,$ | $\,67.505\,$ | $\,63.167\,$ | $\,60.346\,$ | $\,58.164\,$ |

So, we have

$$
P(Y\ge 60.346)=0.15
$$

which means

$$
P(Y\le 60.346)=0.85.
$$

Therefore, $y=60.346.$"} {:db/id 17592186048735} {:db/id 17592186048984} {:db/id 17592186049717} {:db/id 17592186049985} {:db/id 17592186050079} {:db/id 17592186049815 :topic/difficulty  Find $\text{Var}[3X+2Y].$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y].
$$

Also, the variance of $X$ is determined by the formula 

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{X}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =1\cdot 0.2+2\cdot 0.3+3\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.3\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x) \\  & =1\cdot 0.2+4\cdot 0.3+9\cdot 0.5 \\  & =5.9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =5.9-{2.3}^{2} \\  & =0.61.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{Y}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}y\cdot f(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 0.75 \\  & =1.75\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}{y}^{2}\cdot f(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.25+4\cdot 0.75 \\  & =3.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =3.25-{1.75}^{2} \\  & =0.1875.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X-2Y] & ={3}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{2}^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & ={3}^{2}(0.61)+{2}^{2}(0.1875) \\  & =6.24.\end{aligned}

$$
\text{Var}[aX+bY]={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{b}^{2}\text{Var}[Y].
$$

Also, the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula 

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

First, let's find $\text{Var}[X]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =70-{8}^{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =130-{11}^{2} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[4X-\frac{1}{3}Y] & ={4}^{2}\text{Var}[X]+{(-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}\text{Var}[Y] \\  & =16\cdot 6+\frac{1}{9}\cdot 9 \\  & =97.\end{aligned}

a set $S.$

The values $\textrm{E}[X]$ and $\textrm{E}[X^2]$ are called the **first moment** and **second moment** of $X,$ respectively. 

Recall that the first moment $\textrm{E}[X]$ is also called the *expected value* of $X$ and is computed as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X] = \int_S x \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

To find second moment $\textrm{E}[X^2],$ the expected value of the the random variable $X^2,$ we simply substitute $x^2$ for $x$ in the formula above, as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \textrm{E}[X^2] = \int_S x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

Let's compute the second moment $\textrm{E}[X^2]$ of the continuous random variable $X$ with the probability density function 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}, \qquad 0 \leq x \leq 1.
$$

We compute the expected value of $X^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{2}{7}{x}^{7/2}){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{2}{7}-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2847fd82-e842-5ae8-889a-66f29c0442ec" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6591 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3dc1ae12-0989-5596-8114-7d74427919d2" :step/math-academy-id $$
\textrm{E}[X^n] = \int_S x^n \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x.

$$
\textrm{E}[X], \quad \textrm{E}[X^2], \quad \textrm{E}[X^3], \quad \ldots
$$

are sometimes referred to as the first, second, and third **raw moments**. This is because it's possible to define other types of moments.

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}]=10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2\,\text{d}x \\  & =2x\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=2$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[10-4{X}^{2}] & =10-4\text{E}[{X}^{2}] \\  & =10-4\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "46c499f6-0d50-5bd9-9f52-26ed8cb8ebb6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186479153}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1cfd005b-75a8-5b0f-ba56-4a0ed93ab33a" :answer/type {:db/id "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5},\,0<x<1
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20},$ compute $\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+\text{E}[1] \\  & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the third raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{3{x}^{2}+4}{5})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5}+\frac{4}{5}{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{10}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{5}{x}^{4})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{20}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{3}]=\frac{3}{10}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X-{X}^{3}+1] & =2\text{E}[X]-\text{E}[{X}^{3}]+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{11}{20}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{11}{10}-\frac{3}{10}+1 \\  & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "473a0974-6e51-5843-94d7-0cf17d7cd776" :step/next {:db/id 17592186479149}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a69b927d-fd51-516f-aae0-cf0da09a7720" :answer/type {:db/id $$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=e-1,$ compute $\text{E}[2{X}^{2}-X].$

$$
\text{E}[2{X}^{2}-X]=2\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=e-1$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2{X}^{2}-X] & =2\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}-(e-1) \\  & ={e}^{2}-1-e+1 \\  & ={e}^{2}-e.\end{aligned}

$$"} :step/id #uuid "62dbfd8d-d6c8-5022-be2b-1ea1fd60fadf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186508118}} {:db/id 17592186508141 :step/content {:db/id 17592186508093 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b2368f6-3f68-54b0-9d32-a27cbf3895be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}+e-2" :db/id 17592186507648} {:answer/id #uuid "b02c68e4-e61b-5654-9879-70de70a8fe6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}-2e+3" :db/id 17592186507843} {:answer/id #uuid "b269375e-588f-5e5f-9ae9-591c8a3221c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2}-e" :db/id 17592186507845} {:answer/id #uuid "bfd68903-0ef9-5e2a-88ed-3677ac3ae07b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}-e" :db/id 17592186507864} {:answer/id #uuid "c01cb739-f7ab-5ebb-8e34-daf477537efd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2}-5e+3" :db/id 17592186507865}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507864} :answer-field/id #uuid "440eb13c-81c4-5c5d-9faa-611d1e590780" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186507967}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b8f3b4b6-eb37-510a-a5f6-48850ac9d684" :question/math-academy-id "q-131140" :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,1<x<e
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=e-1,$ compute $\text{E}[2{X}^{2}-X].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[2{X}^{2}-X]=2\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=e-1$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2{X}^{2}-X] & =2\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}-(e-1) \\  & ={e}^{2}-1-e+1 \\  & ={e}^{2}-e.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "81573813-f419-5bab-b167-8255dfe1a85b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186508152}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b2368f6-3f68-54b0-9d32-a27cbf3895be" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-131142" :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2},\,1<x<3
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=2,$ compute $\text{E}[5X-3{X}^{2}].$

*Hint: You may assume that $\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y]$ for any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the hint and the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[5X-3{X}^{2}]=5\text{E}[X]-3\text{E}[{X}^{2}]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\,|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=2$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{13}{3}$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[5X-3{X}^{2}] & =5\text{E}[X]-3\text{E}[{X}^{2}] \\  & =5\cdot 2-3\cdot \frac{13}{3} \\  & =10-13 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b234828c-5807-5de4-a2a5-5f231ccf4ede" :step/next {:db/id 17592186508137}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13ed44a6-241d-5838-9fc9-af9b6f83e61d" :answer/type {:db/id :tutorial/content "The partial derivative of a function exists where the original function is defined *and* the partial derivative is defined.

For example, let's consider the function $f(x,y) = \ln(xy).$ We wish to determine the set of values $(x,y)$ on which the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists.

First, we need to find the domain of $f$ since we cannot differentiate $f$ at any point that lies outside of its domain. The natural logarithm is defined only for positive inputs, so the domain of $f$ is 

$$
D_f = \{ (x,y)\, : \, xy > 0 \}.
$$

Next, we compute the partial derivative:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

The partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ (also denoted $f_x$) is not defined at $x=0.$ So, the domain of $f_x$ is

$$
D_{f_x} = \{ (x,y)\, : \, x \ne 0 \}.
$$

To compute the set where  $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists, we take the intersection of the domain of the original function $(D_f)$ with the domain of the partial derivative $(D_{f_x})$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists on the set $\{ (x,y)\, : \, xy \gt 0 \}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5862db65-6f2d-5256-968d-cb971dd6b2f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2532 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125314}} {:db/id 17592186125314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125742 :tutorial/content "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

But for a multivariable function, even if all partial derivatives are defined at a certain point, it **does not mean** that the function is continuous at that point!

The reason why partial differentiability does not imply continuity in the case of a multivariable function is that

- the existence of the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ depend only on the behavior of $f$ parallel to the $x$- and $y$-axes, whereas

- the continuity of $f$ depends on its behavior as we approach $(x_0,y_0)$ from any direction.

For example, let's consider the following multivariable function:

![](images/cb/cb5aad599789d1e317ff3ddc07eaa418e80469307f67e98e2108660fc7d15701.svg)

The function $f$ is defined at the point $(0,0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f(0,0)=0
$$

Likewise, the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ are both defined at the point $(0,0).$ We can compute them using the limit definition of the partial derivative, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0+h,0)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(h)(0)}{{h}^{2}+{0}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0,0+h)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(0)(h)}{{0}^{2}+{h}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So the partial derivatives both exist at $(0,0).$ We will now show that the function is not continuous at $(0,0).$

For the function $f$ to be continuous at $(0,0),$ the limit of the function must be equal to the function value, regardless of the path taken. So, we must have

$$
\lim\limits_{(x,y) \to (0,0)}  f(x,y) = f(0,0) =0.
$$

However, this is not the case here. When we evaluate the limit along the path $y=x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (0,0)\,\,y=x}f(x,y) & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{x\cdot x}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function $f(x,y)$ is *not* continuous at the point $(0,0),$ even though both of its partial derivatives exist there." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca47070b-a1d3-53ad-8f57-2dbd4e770dce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2533 :tutorial/title "Partial Differentiability Does Not Imply Continuity"} :step/id #uuid "f23e88d8-c204-5795-b172-b05000a202c3" :step/math-academy-id 11432} {:db/id 17592186125463 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124557 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124366 :question/id #uuid "97192aac-6c1a-5ead-962b-0bf7ab573661" :question/math-academy-id "e-6109"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2d7d4db-e9e1-54a0-aadb-42447771855d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125001} {:db/id 17592186125193} {:db/id 17592186268902} {:db/id 17592186268903} {:db/id 17592186268904} {:db/id 17592186339043} {:db/id 17592186339044} {:db/id 17592186339046} {:db/id 17592186339047} {:db/id 17592186381048} {:db/id 17592186382207} {:db/id 17592186409559} {:db/id 17592186426720} {:db/id 17592186436749} {:db/id 17592186436751}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist"} :step/id #uuid "c86dfe84-cedf-55cf-bf44-efb12a49ac66" :step/math-academy-id 22675 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125313}}] :activity/title "Partial Differentiability of Multivariable Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124725} {:db/id 17592186125311 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125741 :tutorial/content "The partial derivative of a function exists where the original function is defined *and* the partial derivative is defined.

\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists on the set $\{ (x,y)\, : \, xy \gt 0 \}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5862db65-6f2d-5256-968d-cb971dd6b2f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2532 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e4bac5fb-b77d-59b1-8380-2ff0cf754d5c" :step/math-academy-id 11425 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125312}} {:db/id 17592186125741 :tutorial/content "The partial derivative of a function exists where the original function is defined *and* the partial derivative is defined.

For example, let's consider the function $f(x,y) = \ln(xy).$ We wish to determine the set of values $(x,y)$ on which the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists.

First, we need to find the domain of $f$ since we cannot differentiate $f$ at any point that lies outside of its domain. The natural logarithm is defined only for positive inputs, so the domain of $f$ is 

$$
D_f = \{ (x,y)\, : \, xy > 0 \}.
$$

Next, we compute the partial derivative:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

The partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ (also denoted $f_x$) is not defined at $x=0.$ So, the domain of $f_x$ is

$$
D_{f_x} = \{ (x,y)\, : \, x \ne 0 \}.
$$

To compute the set where  $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists, we take the intersection of the domain of the original function $(D_f)$ with the domain of the partial derivative $(D_{f_x})$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists on the set $\{ (x,y)\, : \, xy \gt 0 \}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5862db65-6f2d-5256-968d-cb971dd6b2f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2532 17592186125314}} {:db/id 17592186125314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125742 :tutorial/content "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

But for a multivariable function, even if all partial derivatives are defined at a certain point, it **does not mean** that the function is continuous at that point!

The reason why partial differentiability does not imply continuity in the case of a multivariable function is that

- the existence of the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ depend only on the behavior of $f$ parallel to the $x$- and $y$-axes, whereas

- the continuity of $f$ depends on its behavior as we approach $(x_0,y_0)$ from any direction.

For example, let's consider the following multivariable function:

![](images/cb/cb5aad599789d1e317ff3ddc07eaa418e80469307f67e98e2108660fc7d15701.svg)

The function $f$ is defined at the point $(0,0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f(0,0)=0
$$

Likewise, the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ are both defined at the point $(0,0).$ We can compute them using the limit definition of the partial derivative, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0+h,0)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(h)(0)}{{h}^{2}+{0}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0,0+h)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(0)(h)}{{0}^{2}+{h}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So the partial derivatives both exist at $(0,0).$ We will now show that the function is not continuous at $(0,0).$

For the function $f$ to be continuous at $(0,0),$ the limit of the function must be equal to the function value, regardless of the path taken. So, we must have

$$
\lim\limits_{(x,y) \to (0,0)}  f(x,y) = f(0,0) =0.
$$

However, this is not the case here. When we evaluate the limit along the path $y=x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (0,0)\,\,y=x}f(x,y) & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{x\cdot x}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function $f(x,y)$ is *not* continuous at the point $(0,0),$ even though both of its partial derivatives exist there." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca47070b-a1d3-53ad-8f57-2dbd4e770dce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2533 :tutorial/title "Partial Differentiability Does Not Imply Continuity"} :step/id #uuid "f23e88d8-c204-5795-b172-b05000a202c3" :step/math-academy-id 11432} {:db/id 17592186125742 :tutorial/content "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

"q-72010" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,-1)$

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(1,-1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)}}=-{e}^{\sqrt{-1}}
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}={e}^{1}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=-\frac{e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot \frac{{e}^{\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}}{2\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}=\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II  only'."} :step/id #uuid "06a4b700-aa67-595f-ad77-c3a9c2d08fa3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409563}} {:db/id 17592186409561 :step/content {:db/id 17592186339043 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8b4579a6-884f-5620-9c48-03f859207fbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}" :db/id 17592186337292} {:answer/id #uuid "aa211335-2ec0-5533-aaf0-0747d0111e9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ge 0}" :db/id 17592186337566} {:answer/id #uuid "ab12ccaa-59a3-5391-8885-0e57cfa9220d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<0}" :db/id 17592186337575} {:answer/id #uuid "d30b5af1-be96-52a2-983e-53d94d787930" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186337875} {:answer/id #uuid "d932ef34-432a-58eb-96dc-98456b7b3465" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0}" :db/id 17592186337921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337292} :answer-field/id #uuid "167ce942-9903-5739-b46e-634adbd1db2c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338315}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "329fb25a-c39e-587a-8c51-720f867dc9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72005" :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y)=\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1786d23c-6b2b-5b25-8a34-a3df54af58bf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409560}} {:db/id 17592186409562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186335822 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "39c4f7c1-2cc1-57ed-a18b-bf91992e00d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451483} {:answer/id #uuid "f3e4c2de-8568-5ff2-baf8-40d15c25b5ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451484}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451484} :answer-field/id #uuid "99c60c75-d597-5852-8b29-5420ba46e80b" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452589} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "96e8d67b-c006-521e-ad4e-1b3b5e5bbae0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451485} {:answer/id #uuid "5fcff0a4-c6d8-5ff7-9344-ecba3634e8b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451486}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451485} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf8a887b-1bb0-5b36-af98-54f46b4ff833" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452590} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bd09d87-8f09-5958-88e2-49043d0205b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451487} {:answer/id #uuid "72089ef2-d948-531c-b1f3-ac84e9dc1b0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451488}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451488} :answer-field/id #uuid "6d4fe7e1-7135-5cca-a3a0-20d39be1b879" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452591}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b22bd39f-49d5-56c7-8797-705e83876e55" :question/math-academy-id "q-65255" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=xy{e}^{x/y}?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${f}_{x}(0,1)$is defined

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(1,0)$ is defined

- **III.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+x{e}^{x/y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}{e}^{x/y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=0\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{0/1}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot {e}^{0/1}+0\cdot {e}^{0/1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into ${f}_{y}$, we get

$$
{f}_{y}(1,0)=1\cdot {e}^{1/0}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{0}\cdot {e}^{1/0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1)=1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}+1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=2e \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{1}\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e-e=0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z},

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $xyz>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$

$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.\end{aligned}

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,\sqrt{3})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} :step/id #uuid "be87cbb6-8a21-5895-a193-08d9d1a311c5"}] :activity/title "Partial Differentiability of Multivariable Functions" :activity/type 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0a3b6388-98bd-5083-8d1c-f60a05890b23" :question/math-academy-id "q-132726" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
- **III.** ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,\sqrt{3})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} :step/id #uuid "be87cbb6-8a21-5895-a193-08d9d1a311c5"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e148fac7-727b-55d9-ba67-0a9fc7a276e4" "q-72022" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy(z-1))?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The partial derivative with respect to $z$ is defined at $(3,2,1)$

- **II.** ${f}_{y}(1,1,2)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{x}(1,2,3)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot y(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot x(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot xy \\  & =\frac{1}{z-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.  

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(3,2,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(3,2,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot 2\cdot (1-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined.

- Statement II is true. If we substitute $(1,1,2)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,1,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot (2-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1,2) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. If we substitute $(1,2,3)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,2,3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 2\cdot (3-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4),
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,2,3) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III  only'."} :step/id #uuid "30fe1f41-c7f8-5010-a260-ed3ef63a4abc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426726}} {:db/id 17592186426723 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268914 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "be072909-07f4-5637-903f-a70436d30a22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449508} {:answer/id #uuid "049c935c-a4ee-5a02-b019-9fd190c4913a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449509}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449509} :answer-field/id #uuid "548fb633-f107-5482-81d5-3893faff9da9" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450708} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6299e699-f9eb-5bb0-bad6-16b58253ff62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449510} {:answer/id #uuid "1a54ebb4-bb0e-5d8c-89d3-811768de2241" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449511}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449510} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8cc1d60-0069-586b-b1d2-3edcc2ab8a3a" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450709} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c3e18ad-85a1-5207-a031-4d811fa7f0dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449512} {:answer/id #uuid "b0e9a6dd-aa8d-53df-aa34-38929292da67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449513}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449512} :answer-field/id #uuid "abb845e0-0f31-593e-85f2-f6c94ef89a74" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450710}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a68d3690-fbcf-53d1-acbf-a5134efed5cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-132728" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2)?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(0,2)$

- **II.** ${f}_{x}(1,0)$ is defined

- **III.** ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} :step/id #uuid "574ad7f2-698f-50d6-8eee-36f6145d16e5"} {:db/id 17592186426724 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125001 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "323e1e26-806d-5103-9c5b-05be999f86f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}" :db/id 17592186426704} {:answer/id #uuid "3f71ffa0-c375-5e54-a4b4-82c47e1862fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0<xyz<1\}" :db/id 17592186426705} {:answer/id #uuid "58a495bb-1535-5c0c-8153-9cddc1a1d72c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186426707} {:answer/id #uuid "66b51739-6d9c-59ee-81d0-4f21e588a03b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}" :db/id 17592186426708} {:answer/id #uuid "ab77e5e6-52f4-5889-9394-0781e3a0ecd5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}" :db/id 17592186426711}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426704} :answer-field/id #uuid "6476017e-359c-522d-8dec-b6d7cd0832c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186122606}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f23029a5-0003-5b31-a62a-a58e0c29de2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-36527" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{xz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $-1\le xyz\le 1.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}}$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(xyz)^{2} & >0 \\ (xyz)^{2} & <1 \\ |xyz| & <1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives $-1<xyz<1.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d1a2f4bc-c2ad-5ea9-bbc9-a5f92a8d1b61" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426725}} {:db/id 17592186426725 :step/content {:db/id 17592186426721 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26545a18-833f-5099-8272-edbb2a66edaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426703} {:answer/id #uuid "4d5bdc4f-f2f7-5295-b2ba-aa4588793c88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,xy\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186426706} {:answer/id #uuid "a9d10897-b8cf-5fad-b81e-91fbcac64c00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{y}$ exists everywhere on the $xy$-plane" :db/id 17592186426710} {:answer/id #uuid "ebb0a6cd-e867-5b85-88ef-cd845e6904a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,xy<0\}" :db/id 17592186426714} {:answer/id #uuid "ff439fa7-e5eb-53d6-8dc0-e5396941eb06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}" :db/id 17592186426717}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426717} :answer-field/id #uuid "4cca11fe-f3bb-53ee-b7b6-de2725b37ad7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426718}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "abe73768-66b7-589e-98db-9176084649e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-72006" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{x}{xy} \\  & =\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is defined only for

$$
\begin{aligned}y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d34189a3-bcaf-5744-9e6b-ec97ad8307d1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426722}} {:db/id 17592186426726 :step/content {:db/id 17592186426720 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9a414987-4111-5550-9b84-35b48e518248" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426709} {:answer/id #uuid "c4574d37-c2e2-5922-8956-3143f5bef26f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y>0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426712} {:answer/id #uuid "c67ec9fa-9f76-59b9-b6ed-a85557705824" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y>0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426713} {:answer/id #uuid "ee7e5c9b-05ac-5232-9af8-bc55f1d66335" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426715} {:answer/id #uuid "f480f4b0-b440-57d3-be41-894b18986911" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426716}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426716} :answer-field/id #uuid "4d0f4a07-8c58-5c53-b0aa-71dedf0ab601" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426719}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13585dd1-9ab5-5887-870c-2d899c40d4a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-132652" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ and

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is

$$

$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{y{sin}^{2}⁡z}
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "dd470b32-cbc1-54d2-9ca1-54631aa728a9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426723}} {:db/id 17592186426723 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268914 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "be072909-07f4-5637-903f-a70436d30a22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449508} {:answer/id #uuid "049c935c-a4ee-5a02-b019-9fd190c4913a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449509}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449509} :answer-field/id #uuid "548fb633-f107-5482-81d5-3893faff9da9" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450708} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6299e699-f9eb-5bb0-bad6-16b58253ff62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449510} {:answer/id #uuid "1a54ebb4-bb0e-5d8c-89d3-811768de2241" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449511}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449510} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8cc1d60-0069-586b-b1d2-3edcc2ab8a3a" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450709} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c3e18ad-85a1-5207-a031-4d811fa7f0dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186449512} {:answer/id #uuid "b0e9a6dd-aa8d-53df-aa34-38929292da67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186449513}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186449512} :answer-field/id #uuid "abb845e0-0f31-593e-85f2-f6c94ef89a74" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186450710}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a68d3690-fbcf-53d1-acbf-a5134efed5cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-132728" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2)?$
